description: the Cham king consecrates the Śaiva dynastic sanctuary of Champa, fusing his own name with Śiva as the liṅga-cult Bhadreśvara
source: Cham Sanskrit inscriptions; [scholarly] late 4th c. CE

title: Bhāgyacandra stages the first Manipuri Rāsa-līlā
description: the Meitei king choreographs Kṛṣṇa's rāsa from a dream-vision for the Govindajī temple (1779 CE) [regional]

title: Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu completed at Vṛndāvana
description: Rūpa Gosvāmī finishes the four-division 'ocean' that makes Kṛṣṇa-rati itself the sthāyi-bhāva and bhakti the supreme rasa (Śaka 1463 = 1541 CE, per colophon)

title: Bhaktiranna's cloud-chariot return
description: hearing of the heroes' deaths at Kasi, the pilgrim uncle Bhaktiranna returns in a cloud-chariot, frees the confined Papanuka, orders sati on the Yadava women and performs pinda offerings on the Paleru

title: Bhāṇḍu Datta's treachery and Kālketu's capture
description: The corrupt kāyastha Bhāṇḍu Datta instigates the Kālinga king to invade Gujarāṭ; Kālketu is captured, then freed when Caṇḍī commands the king in a dream

title: Bhānudās restores the image from Vijayanagara (16th c.)
description: Vārkarī hagiography tells that the Viṭṭhala image, carried to Vijayanagara, was brought back to Pandharpur by Bhānudās, great-grandfather of Eknāth

title: Bharata's rasa-sūtra codified
description: the Nāṭya Śāstra defines rasa as arising from vibhāva, anubhāva and vyabhicāri-bhāva, the secular apparatus later transposed onto devotion (c. 200 BCE–200 CE [scholarly])

title: Bhāratcandra composes the Annadāmaṅgal (1752)
description: the poet Bhāratcandra Rāy "Rāy-Guṇākar" completes the last and most polished Bengali maṅgal-kāvya at the Nadia court, glorifying the goddess Annadā (Annapūrṇā)

title: Bhāravi composes the Kirātārjunīya
description: 18-canto mahākāvya on Arjuna's duel with Śiva-as-hunter, c. 6th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Bhāsa dramatizes the saga
description: the Trivandrum plays attributed to Bhāsa stage the capture in Pratijñāyaugandharāyaṇa and the fire-ruse and dream-scene in Svapnavāsavadatta, his acknowledged masterpiece

title: Bhāsa's plays composed
description: thirteen dramas reshaping epic material (Ūrubhaṅga's dying Duryodhana, Karṇabhāra, Pañcarātra's averted war), dated anywhere from c. 2nd c. BCE to the early centuries CE [scholarly] [disputed]

title: Bhāskararāya completes the Saubhāgya-bhāskara (c. 1728 CE)
description: the great Śrī-Vidyā systematizer (1690–1785) writes the standard commentary on the thousand names, fixing the received text and its Śrī-cakra/Pañcadaśī reading [scholarly]

title: Bhaṭṭi composes the Bhaṭṭikāvya at Valabhī
description: 22-canto Rāvaṇavadha telling the Rāmāyaṇa while exemplifying Pāṇini's grammar, c. 7th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Bhavabhūti stages the Uttararāmacarita
description: court poet of Yaśovarman of Kanyākubja (early 8th c. CE [scholarly]) rewrites the Sītā-abandonment with a reunion happy ending via Vālmīki's play-within-a-play

title: Bhavānanda aids Mān Siṃha (c. 1600 CE)
description: the goddess's devotee Bhavānanda Majumdār supports the Mughal general Mān Siṃha's campaign against the Bengal rebel Pratāpāditya of Jessore

title: Bhoja unearths Vikramāditya's throne
description: reports of a mound that made a cowherd judge like a king lead the Paramāra Bhoja of Dhārā to excavate the buried siṃhāsana borne on thirty-two statuettes and attempt to be enthroned

title: Biroba enthroned at Ārevāḍī
description: the shepherd-god's great cult-centre rises at Ārevāḍī in Sāngli district, focus of the Dhangar Biroba ovī and vigil-worship

title: Birth of Tejaji at Kharnal
description: the Jat hero Vir Teja is born to Taharji and Ramkunwari of the Dhauliya clan, by folk reckoning in V.S. 1130 (1074 CE) [folk] [disputed]

title: Birth of Tulsīdās
description: the future poet-saint is born (trad. V.S. 1589 / 1532 CE, birth-year disputed) at Rājāpur under the inauspicious Abhuktamūla nakṣatra, speaking "Rāma" as his first word
source: Mūla Gosāīṃ Carita [late text]; Wikipedia, Tulsidas

title: Birth of Vedānta Deśika at Tūppul
description: Veṅkaṭanātha, the future kavi-tārkika-siṃha, is born near Kāñcīpuram in 1268 [traditional]

title: Blackburn documents the bow-song tradition
description: Stuart Blackburn's late-1970s Tirunelveli fieldwork and Singing of Birth and Death (1988) record the vil pāṭṭu genre, its birth-vs-death story types and the Muttuppaṭṭaṉ Katai in English
source: Blackburn, Singing of Birth and Death, 1988

title: Bodāṇā's tulsī yātrā
description: the aged Ḍākor Rājpūt Bodāṇā walks to Dvārakā twice a year carrying holy basil for Raṇchhoḍrāī, keeping the vow into his seventies

title: Brahma-vaivarta Rādhā-tattva codified
description: the Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa in its received form (c. 15th–16th c. CE) gives Rādhā her full cosmic theology of Goloka, the Pañca-prakṛti and supremacy over Vaikuṇṭha

title: Buddhabhatta composes the Ratnapariksha
description: The fullest classical Sanskrit lapidary carrying the Bala gem-origin myth is composed in the mid-first millennium CE (Gupta horizon), later edited by Louis Finot (1896) [scholarly]
source: Buddhabhatta, Ratnapariksha; Finot, Les lapidaires indiens

title: Budhasvāmin's Bṛhatkathāślokasaṃgraha composed
description: a Nepalese-transmitted, first-person verse epitome of the lost Bṛhatkathā (c. 8th–9th c. CE, date disputed), lacking the Kailāsa frame and argued by Lacôte to stand closest to Guṇāḍhya's original

title: Burzōy's Pahlavi translation
description: the physician Burzōy carries the Panchatantra into Middle Persian at the Sasanian court, c. 550 CE [scholarly], parent of the lost Pahlavi and surviving Syriac versions

title: Caitanya instructs Rūpa at Prayāga
description: ten days of teaching at Daśāśvamedha-ghāṭ plant the seed of bhakti-rasa doctrine and dispatch Rūpa to Vṛndāvana (1516 CE [late text])

title: Caitanya re-identifies Rādhā-kuṇḍa
description: on his Braj pilgrimage c. 1515 CE, Caitanya Mahāprabhu locates the lost Rādhā-kuṇḍa in paddy-fields, and his Gosvāmī disciples systematize the hlādinī-śakti theology of Rādhā

title: Caitanya relishes Vidyāpati's padas at Purī
description: in the 16th century Caitanya Mahāprabhu tastes Vidyāpati's songs day and night alongside Jayadeva and Caṇḍīdāsa, launching the Brajabuli imitation-corpus under the poet's signature

title: Calon Arang unleashes plague under Airlangga (setting: 11th c.; oldest MS 1540 CE)
description: the widow-witch of Girah worships Durgā and ravages the kingdom until the sage Mpu Bharadah defeats her, the tale behind Bali's Rangda mask [regional]

title: Caṇḍeśa canonized as the 20th Nāyaṉār
description: named in Sundarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai and versified by Cēkkiḻār as the 20th of the 63 Nāyaṉār lives in the Periya Purāṇam (c. 1135 CE)

title: Caṇḍī rescues Śrīmanta at the execution-ground
description: Śrīmanta, condemned in Ceylon like his father, is saved when Caṇḍī's host routs the king's men; the king worships her, is granted the Kamale-Kāminī vision, frees Dhanapati and weds Suśīlā to Śrīmanta

title: Caṇḍī reveals herself as the golden iguana to Kālketu
description: The goddess, caught by the hunter Kālketu as a golden monitor-lizard tied with his bowstring, reveals her four-armed form and gives him a priceless ring and treasure

title: Caṇḍīmaṅgal dramatizes Maṅgalā Caṇḍī
description: Mukundarāma's late-16th-c. Bengali maṅgal-kāvya recasts the fortune-goddess as the deity who compels worship from the hunter Kālketu and the merchant Dhanapati

title: Canonization as Tirumurai Book 12 (by c. 1313 CE)
description: Umāpati Śivācārya's Cēkkiḻār Purāṇam records the composition legend, by which time the epic is fixed as the twelfth book of the Śaiva canon [scholarly]

title: Cāntu's betrayal and the dying hero
description: the wounded victor sends Cāntu to fetch his people, but the kinsman-traitor instead strips the dying Ārōmal of his gold ring and carries home a lying account

title: Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi codified
description: Hemādri, minister of the Yādavas of Devagiri, writes the largest of all nibandhas, whose Vrata-khaṇḍa catalogs hundreds of vows and festivals

title: Cēkkiḻār composes the Periya Purāṇam (c. 1135 CE)
description: the chief minister, given the grace-word "Ulagelām" by Śiva at Chidambaram per later legend, premieres the 4,286-verse epic in the Thousand-Pillared Hall under Kulōttuṅga II [scholarly]

title: Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ consecrates the Pattini temple at Vañci
description: The Chera king brings Himalayan stone and enshrines Kaṇṇaki as Pattini at Vañci — traditionally identified with Kodungallur — with Gajabāhu of Laṅkā attending (the disputed c. 2nd-century-CE synchronism)

title: Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ's Himalayan stone expedition
description: the Chera king marches north, defeats the Āryan kings Kanaka and Vijaya, and has them carry back on their heads the Himalayan stone, Gaṅgā-bathed, for Pattini's image

title: Chaitanya relishes the Gīta-Govinda at Purī (c. 1510–1534 CE)
description: Caitanya Mahāprabhu tastes Jayadeva's songs day and night with Svarūpa Dāmodara and Rāmānanda Rāya, making the poem the emotional textbook of Gauḍīya Rādhā-bhāva

title: Charter of the Khudurukuṇī Oṣā
description: Because Maṅgaḷā accepted a wronged girl's broken rice and set her world right, unmarried girls of coastal Odisha keep the goddess's oṣā on the Sundays of Bhādraba, offering khuda and reciting the Tāpoi kathā for their brothers' welfare
source: Khudurukuṇī Oṣā observance, Odia folk tradition

title: Charter of the tulasī-exclusion in Gaṇeśa-pūjā
description: The curse-exchange becomes the standing ritual rule barring tulasī leaves from Gaṇeśa worship (dūrvā grass offered instead), with a contested folk exception on Gaṇeśa Caturthī

title: Chemmarathi's curse and self-immolation
description: hearing of his death Chemmarathi curses in grief and throws herself onto her husband's funeral pyre

title: Chempakasseri absorbed by Travancore (c. 1746 CE)
description: the Ambalappuzha principality that raised and endowed the temple is annexed by Marthanda Varma's expanding Travancore

title: Chempakasseri Krishna enshrined at Ambalappuzha
description: the Chempakasseri king Devanarayanan Thampuran installs Krishna as Parthasarathi, whip and conch in hand, as the kingdom's tutelary deity

title: Cīrāḷaṉ runs in alive
description: at his mother's call the sacrificed boy comes running home whole and living, and the Bhairava and the curry both vanish

title: Ciṟuttoṇṭar at Vātāpi (642 CE)
description: general Paranjōti takes Vātāpi for the Pallavas [scholarly], then retires to the sainthood crowned by the child-curry ordeal

title: Ciṟuttoṇṭar named in the Tiruttoṇṭattokai
description: Sundarar honours the child-curry devotee in verse 6 of his roll-call hymn, the seed-list from which the 63-Nāyaṉār canon was later fixed

title: Ciṟuttoṇṭar's feeding-vow
description: the retired general vows never to eat without first feeding a devotee of Śiva, keeping the vow with his wife Veṇkāṭṭu Nangai, son Cīrāḷaṉ, and servant at Tirucceṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi

title: Cōḻa foundation of the shrine
description: the stone temple over the sacred well is traditionally endowed by the Cōḻa emperor Kulottuṅga Cōḻa I in the late 11th century CE

title: Colonial suppression of Charak hook-swinging (1865)
description: The Bengal government prohibits the hook-swinging ordeal of the Gajan–Charak Puja; the rite goes underground and persists only patchily

title: Compilation of the Garuḍa Purāṇa's Preta-khaṇḍa
description: the death-rite section accretes onto the layered first-millennium-CE Purāṇa (core estimates 4th–11th c., developed form by c. 900–1000 CE) [scholarly]

title: Composition and stratification of the Padma Purāṇa
description: [scholarly] the text compiles across roughly the 4th–15th c. CE (core c. 750–1000 CE), diverging into a Bengal 5-khaṇḍa and a printed 6-khaṇḍa recension with the Kriyāyogasāra-khaṇḍa as a late seventh supplement

title: Composition of the Acchodā Pitṛ-kalpa accounts
description: The Harivaṃśa (c. 1st–3rd c. CE onward) and the Matsya Purāṇa's early core (c. 200–500 CE) commit the Acchodā–Satyavatī rebirth frame to writing as śrāddha doctrine [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Asya Vamasya riddle hymn (RV 1.164)
description: The 52-verse brahmodya attributed to Dirghatamas, containing the two-birds verse (1.164.20) and 'ekam sad vipra bahudha vadanti' (1.164.46), is composed in the later Rigvedic period, c. 1200-1000 BCE [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Skandha 11)
description: [scholarly] dating places the Purāṇa, with its Nimi saṃvāda and southern river-praise, c. 8th–10th century CE, likely in the Tamil south

title: Composition of the Bhāgavata-Māhātmya (c. 16th–18th c. CE) [scholarly]
description: The Māhātmya enters the Padma Purāṇa's Uttara-khaṇḍa as a late addition, dated by scholars (Hawley) to early-modern North India, its Bhakti-journey verse becoming the charter of the 'bhakti movement' idea and of the modern saptāha
source: Padma Purāṇa, Uttara-khaṇḍa 193–198; Hawley, A Storm of Songs

title: Composition of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa's Tulasī–Gaṇeśa saṃvāda
description: The extant Bengal recension containing the Gaṇapati-khaṇḍa dialogue is dated c. 15th–16th century CE, with possible earlier strata [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Cilappatikāram
description: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ's epic of Kaṇṇaki, charter of the Pattini/Bhagavati assimilation, is composed — traditionally c. 100–250 CE, by modern scholarly consensus c. 5th century CE

title: Composition of the Cūḍālā tale (Mokṣopāya, Kashmir, c. 950 CE)
description: The Cūḍālā-ākhyāna is composed within the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya, later Vedānticized into the vulgate Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha by c. the 14th century [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Ekādaśī-māhātmya corpus
description: the Padma Purāṇa's Uttara-khaṇḍa māhātmyas, the Kriyāyogasāra cycle, and the Nārada Purāṇa's Rukmāṅgada legend are judged post-1000 CE vrata literature of the medieval Vaiṣṇava fasting economy

title: Composition of the Gambler's Lament
description: a gambler's confession of ruin by the vibhidaka-nut dice, ending in Savitr's counsel 'play not with dice; plough your field,' composed in the late Mandala 10 stratum c. 1200–1000 BCE [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Gīta-Govinda (c. 1170–1200 CE)
description: Jayadeva composes the 12-sarga / 24-aṣṭapadī Sanskrit lyric, opening with the Daśāvatāra-stotra, in the milieu of Lakṣmaṇasena's Bengal court [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Kālikā Purāṇa in Kāmarūpa
description: the fullest telling of the Lauhitya birth-legend is composed in Assam c. 10th–11th century CE [scholarly]

title: Composition of the māsa-māhātmya strata
description: the month-glorification layers of the Padma and Skanda Purāṇas take shape as late-medieval vrata literature, the Puruṣottama-māhātmya latest of all [scholarly]
source: Hazra, Purāṇic Records; Rocher, The Purāṇas

title: Composition of the Mokṣopāya / Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha
description: The anonymous Kashmiri Mokṣopāya is composed c. 950 CE and later Vedānticized into the vulgate Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha attributed to Vālmīki, its ~25 nested parables carrying the ajāta-vāda doctrine [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra
description: the 84 aphorisms on parā-prema, the eleven āsaktis and gauṇī vs parā bhakti crystallize, commonly dated c. 10th–12th c. CE, post-Bhāgavata [late text] [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Nīlamata Purāṇa
description: Kashmir's charter text — origin myth, nāga-spring roster, and festival calendar — is composed in the valley c. 6th–8th century CE [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Nyāya-sudhā
description: Jayatīrtha writes the "Nectar of Logic" on Madhva's Anuvyākhyāna, the definitive post-founder work of Dvaita Vedānta, before his death c. 1388 CE [scholarly]
source: Sharma, History of the Dvaita School

title: Composition of the Padma Uttara-khaṇḍa tīrtha-māhātmyas [scholarly]
description: the Puṇḍarīka chapters belong to the Uttara-khaṇḍa's late māhātmya strata of a Purāṇa compiled c. 4th–15th c. CE (core layers c. 750–1000 CE)

title: Composition of the Puruṣa Sūkta
description: The hymn is composed within the late stratum of Ṛgveda maṇḍala 10, c. 1200–1000 BCE [scholarly]

title: Composition of the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra
description: ~100 aphorisms opening "athāto bhakti-jijñāsā" argue bhakti (not jñāna) liberates; dating spans early centuries CE to early 2nd millennium [scholarly] [disputed]

title: Composition of the Sudarśana–Śaśikalā charter narrative
description: the Devī Bhāgavata's compilers (c. 9th–14th century CE [scholarly]) compose Skandha III's original story-plus-vidhi unit to legitimize royal Navarātri and Durgā-pūjā at Benares and Ayodhyā
source: Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Skandha III; Brown 1990; Pintchman 1994

title: Composition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa
description: the core books (Kāṇḍas 2–6) are composed c. 7th–4th c. BCE with the Bāla and Uttara Kāṇḍas as later strata, per the critical-edition consensus [scholarly]

title: Composition of the vānara origin-strata
description: the Bāla- and Uttara-kāṇḍas carrying both vānara origin accounts are dated as later additions to the c. 7th–4th c. BCE core epic [scholarly]

title: Composition of Viṣṇu Purāṇa Aṃśa III's closing orthodoxy narrative
description: the Śatadhanu–Śaibyā parable and its anti-pāṣaṇḍa rules are dated c. 400 BCE–450 CE [scholarly], read as brahmanical boundary polemic against Buddhist/Jain competition

title: Condemned to the stake
description: seized on the Brahmins' complaint, Kāttavarāyaṉ is sentenced to death by impalement, the caste order's verdict on a boundary it cannot forgive

title: Consecration of Pattini at Vañci with Gajabāhu attending
description: Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ enshrines Kaṇṇaki as Pattini at Vañci, with "Kayavāku of sea-girt Laṅkā" among the dignitaries — the disputed Gajabāhu synchronism anchoring the events to c. 2nd c. CE

title: Contest with Sambandāṇḍāṉ
description: at King Prabhuḍa Deva Rāya's court a jealous Śākta rival challenges Aruṇagiri to a contest of deities, and Murugan manifests where the Goddess does not

title: Cradle-birth of Ramdev at Undu-Kashmir
description: Ramdev appears miraculously in the cradle in Ajmal's palace, hailed as Krishna's Kali-yuga avatara, traditionally Bhadrapada shukla 2, V.S. 1409 (c. 1352 CE)

title: Dang Hyang Nirartha arrives in Bali (c. 1537) and attains mokṣa at Uluwatu
description: the last great Javanese brahmin reforms the pedanda priesthood, institutes the padmasana shrine and consecrates the sea-temple chain [traditional]

title: Dāsiā Baurī sends a coconut
description: barred from the sanctum as an untouchable, the Baurī devotee hands his coconut to a mocking Brāhmaṇ pilgrim to offer, insisting the Lord will take it in his own hand

title: Dāyabhāga composed
description: Jīmūtavāhana of Bengal writes the rival inheritance digest holding a son gains no right by birth and heirship follows spiritual benefit (piṇḍa-offering), founding the Bengal school

title: Death against the Kodagu raiders
description: fighting valorously but surrounded, Māndappan is slain and his fingers severed, and he gropes the battlefield for them as he dies

title: Death fighting the cattle-rustlers
description: when raiders drive off the countryside's herds, Muttuppaṭṭaṉ pursues them, fights to recover the cattle and is cut down — the violent, premature death that makes a god
source: Muttuppaṭṭaṉ Katai; Blackburn, Singing of Birth and Death

title: Death of Maṇavāḷa Māmunigaḷ
description: the Teṅkalai consolidator, revered as Rāmānuja reborn, passes at Śrīraṅgam in 1443 [traditional], his aṣṭa-dig-gaja disciples carrying the line onward

title: Death of Tulsīdās at Asī Ghāṭ
description: the poet dies on the Gaṅgā's bank at Vārāṇasī, V.S. 1680 (1623 CE), per the tradition-couplet "saṃvat solaha sau asī...", after composing the Hanumān Bāhuka for his ailing arm

title: Deification of Muttuppaṭṭaṉ as guardian god
description: the martyred brahmin-cobbler becomes a kāval deyvam of the Tirunelveli country, honored at koṭai festivals with bow-song and possession, devotees offering leather sandals at his Tāmraparṇī-country shrine
source: vil pāṭṭu cult tradition; Muttuppaṭṭaṉ shrine tradition, Tirunelveli

title: Deification of the jāgar devtās (Katyūrī–Chand era)
description: the wronged dead of Kumaon — prince Bholānāth, the jogī-lovers Gaṅgānāth and Bhānā, the murdered herdsman Kalbiśṭ — are pacified and enshrined as possession deities

title: Deification of the martyr-couple
description: the fallen hero and self-burning wife are raised to godhood as the theyyam deities Kathivanur Veeran and Chemmarathi
source: K.K.N. Kurup, The Cult of Teyyam

title: Deśika escapes the Śrīraṅgam massacre with the Śrutaprakāśikā
description: hiding among the slain, he saves Sudarśana Sūri's Śrī Bhāṣya sub-commentary and the author's two sons, c. 1327 [traditional]

title: Devī-Bhāgavata Book IX and the Brahmavaivarta Prakṛti-khaṇḍa composed
description: the late Śākta corpus issuing Prakṛti-pedigrees to the Bengal folk goddesses; DBP c. 9th–14th c. CE, extant Brahmavaivarta a 15th–16th-c. Bengal recomposition [scholarly]

title: Dhanapati reconciled and Caṇḍī-pūjā established among merchants
description: The stubborn Śaiva merchant accepts the goddess on seeing her one with Śiva, and her worship is planted in the bāṇik community

title: Dhanapati sees the Kamale-Kāminī and is imprisoned in Ceylon
description: After kicking over Caṇḍī's ghaṭ, the Śaiva merchant beholds the lotus-woman swallowing an elephant at Kālīdaha, cannot show the withheld vision to the Siṁhala king, and is jailed as a liar

title: Dharmasindhu completed
description: Kāśīnātha Upādhyāya writes the practical household ritual manual of the late Peśvā Deccan, still the working authority behind everyday domestic observance

title: Dinā and Bhadrī martyred defending the Musahar hamlets
description: The Musahar brother-heroes of the Kosi belt, champions of their community's fields and honour against demons/oppressors (variant-dependent), die violently in their final battle rather than submit

title: Dinā-Bhadrī deified as ancestral gods of the Musahars
description: After their martyrdom the brothers are worshipped at thān shrines in Musahar tolas of the Kosi country with night-long bhagait possession-singing and offerings of pigs and liquor, outside Brahmin priesthood

title: Dvija Mādhava's Caṇḍīmaṅgal composed
description: The earlier dated recension of the Caṇḍīmaṅgal (Sāradāmaṅgal), internally dated Śaka 1501 = 1579 CE [scholarly]

title: E. B. Cowell translates the Śāṇḍilya sūtra (1878)
description: sūtra-plus-Svapneśvara published in English at Calcutta, opening the text to Western scholarship [scholarly]

title: Earliest claimed grand Durgā Pūjā at Tāherpur (c. 1580 CE)
description: tradition credits zamindar Kaṁsanārāyaṇ of Tāherpur with the first Śāradīyā Durgā Pūjā in near-modern form, a claim rivaled and undocumentable

title: Earliest historical attestation of the Vṛṣṇi cult
description: Pāṇini's Vāsudeva-devotees, the Arthaśāstra's Vṛṣṇi saṅgha, the Besnagar Heliodorus pillar (c. 113 BCE) and the Mora well inscription document early Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa worship [scholarly]

title: Earliest mention of Rādhā's name
description: a single Prakrit verse of Hāla's anthology shows Kṛṣṇa blowing dust from Rādhā's face, the first surviving occurrence of her name (~1st–2nd c. CE)

title: Earliest Saṃkarṣaṇa cult inscriptions [scholarly]
description: the Ghosuṇḍī and Nānāghāṭ inscriptions (c. 2nd–1st century BCE) and the Mora well record invoke Saṃkarṣaṇa with Vāsudeva, attesting Balarāma's worship among the oldest documented Vaiṣṇava cults
source: Ghosuṇḍī, Nānāghāṭ & Mora well inscriptions, epigraphy

title: Edgerton's four recensions of the Vikramacarita
description: the Siṃhāsana-dvātriṃśikā survives in four divergent Sanskrit recensions (Southern, Metrical, Brief, Jainistic), critically edited and translated by Franklin Edgerton as *Vikrama's Adventures* (HOS 26–27, 1926)

title: Eka Dasa Rudra interrupted by the Gunung Agung eruption (1963); completed 1979
description: the once-a-century purification of the eleven Rudras at Pura Besakih is shattered by the volcano's deadly eruption mid-ceremony, then performed anew a cycle later [scholarly]

title: Emergence of the Satya Pīr cult in Bengal
description: the deity of the vrata circulates as the fakir Satya Pīr, worshipped by Hindus and Muslims alike with the śirṇi offering, traceable in Bengali literature from the 16th century

title: Emperor Harṣa writes Nāgānanda, Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā
description: royal playwright of Kanauj (r. 606–647 CE) stages Jīmūtavāhana's self-sacrifice to Garuḍa with a Buddhist benediction [scholarly]

title: Endowments deeded to Caṇḍeśvara
description: in Pallava–Chola epigraphy temple lands are granted "to Caṇḍeśvara" as the temple's legal proprietor, translating his stewardship into property law (e.g. the Bṛhadīśvara, Tañjāvūr)

title: English translations and modern afterlife
description: Burton's retelling (1870), Tawney's translation (1880–84), Ryder's Twenty-two Goblins (1917), Penzer's Ocean of Story (1924–28), and Doordarshan's Vikram aur Betaal (1985) carry the cycle worldwide [scholarly]

title: Enrolled in Sundarar's Tiruttoṇḍattokai
description: Sundarar honours the labourer-saint as "Tirunāḷaippōvār" in his roll-call hymn, the seed-list from which the canonical 63 Nāyaṉārs were later fixed

title: Fables of Bidpai printed in Europe
description: John of Capua's Latin Directorium Humanae Vitae printed 1480 CE [scholarly], spawning the German, Spanish and English (North, 1570) Bidpai lines later credited by La Fontaine

title: Fall of Majapahit and the Hindu exodus to Bali (c. 1478–1527)
description: as Islamic Demak rises, Majapahit's priests, poets and nobles migrate east, making Bali the ark of Javano-Hindu civilization [scholarly]

title: Fall of the Videha monarchy
description: The Arthaśāstra remembers Karāla the Vaideha as destroyed by lust; historically the Videha kingship gives way to the Vajji confederacy centred on Vaiśālī by the Buddha's time [scholarly]

title: Fed at night by the Lord's command
description: moved by the poor man's grief, Jagannātha commands in a servitor's dream that the temple be reopened after hours and Bandhu Mohanty be fed mahāprasāda, the sleeping Lord's kitchen unstopped for one shut-out bhakta

title: First community bāro-yāri pūjā at Guptipara (1790 CE)
description: twelve friends barred from a household pūjā pool subscriptions and hold their own, the first recorded community-subscription Durgā Pūjā

title: First jauhar of Chittor (1303 CE)
description: At ʿAlāʾ-ud-dīn Khaljī's conquest of Chittorgarh the fort's women immolate collectively; later legend centers the fire on queen Padminī via Jāyasī's Padmāvat [disputed] [late text]

title: First print documentation of the Maithili hero-songs (1880s)
description: George A. Grierson's Maithili collections are credited with the earliest recorded specimens of the region's folk songs, including Dinā-Bhadrī material, a century before sustained ethnography

title: First Rāmlīlā instituted at Vārāṇasī
description: tradition credits Tulsīdās and his disciple Megha Bhagat with founding the Rāmlīlā, the open-air enactment of Rāma's story with the Mānas as recited script, ancestor of the Rāmnagar Rāmlīlā and of the form UNESCO honored (2005/2008)
source: UNESCO ICH, Ramlila; Lutgendorf, The Life of a Text [traditional]

title: First sarbajanin (public) pūjā at Bagbazar (1910 CE)
description: the Sanātan Dharmotsāhinī Sabhā holds the first fully public all-comers Durgā Pūjā in Calcutta, the form that became dominant and fused with nationalist Bhārat-Mātā symbolism

title: Gajabāhu brings the Pattini cult to Laṅkā
description: late Sinhala chronicle tradition has Gajabāhu I import Pattini worship and her anklet-relic from the Tamil country, the foundation-legend of the Sinhala cult

title: Gauḍīya deployment of 11.5.32 as Caitanya proof-text
description: the 16th-century Caitanya school reads the saṅkīrtana verse as the Bhāgavata's prophecy of the golden hidden avatāra, canonized in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta

title: Gaura-gaṇoddeśa-dīpikā identifies the Gosvāmīs as mañjarīs
description: Kavi-karṇapūra equates Rūpa with Rūpa-mañjarī, canonizing mañjarī-bhāva as the Gauḍīya siddha identity (1576 CE [late text])

title: Gīta-Govinda canonizes Rādhā
description: Jayadeva's twelve-canto lyric (12th c. CE) makes Rādhā the central heroine of Kṛṣṇa devotion, with Kṛṣṇa begging her foot upon his head, and enters nightly liturgy at Jagannātha Purī

title: Golu Devtā's life and deification (Katyūrī era)
description: the prince born to King Jhāl Rāi and Kālinkā, cast into the river by jealous co-queens, exposes the fraud by the wooden-horse riddle, rules justly, and after death becomes Kumaon's god of justice

title: Gōpālakr̥ṣṇa Bhāratī's Nandaṉ Carittiram (1861)
description: the Tamil composer recasts the Nāyaṉār's life as a Carnatic musical drama that outstrips its scriptural source and makes Nandanar the flashpoint of the caste-and-bhakti debate

title: Gopaṇa restores Raṅganātha to Śrīraṅgam
description: the Vijayanagara commander returns the exiled image c. 1371 and the centenarian Deśika composes praise-verses preserved in epigraphy [scholarly]

title: Gopīcandra's refusal
description: the young enthroned king rejects his mother's demand, disbelieving the prophecy and unable to abandon his queens Aduna and Paduna

title: Gorakhnāth traps the nāgas and Machhindranāth is brought from Kāmarūpa
description: the insulted yogī sits on the rain-serpents causing a twelve-year drought until his guru Matsyendranātha is fetched from Assam and enshrined at Bungamati (legend set under the Licchavi king Narendradeva, trad. 7th c. CE)
source: Kathmandu Valley legend; Newar chronicle tradition

title: Govinda Dīkṣita builds the tank maṇḍapas (early 17th c.)
description: the Thanjavur Nāyak minister renovates the Mahāmaham tank and raises its sixteen maṇḍapas, fixing the festival's built stage

title: Grierson recovers the Rangpur song
description: G. A. Grierson publishes a Rangpur singer's Māṇik Chandra Rājār Gān in 1878, the foundational scholarly text later expanded by D. C. Sen's Gopīcandrer Gān (c. 1922–24)

title: Guṇāḍhya composes the Bṛhatkathā in Paiśācī
description: bound by his lost grammar-wager to renounce Sanskrit, Prakrit and his own tongue, Guṇāḍhya hears the tale from Kāṇabhūti in the Vindhya forest and writes 700,000 ślokas in his own blood over seven years

title: Guruvayur idol sheltered from Tipu (1789 CE)
description: as Tipu Sultan's forces raid Malabar, the Guruvayur processional image is evacuated south and given refuge at Ambalappuzha until worship is restored after 1792

title: Guruvāyūr Kesavan dies in praṇāma on Ekādaśī (2 December 1976 CE)
description: the Gajarājan, gifted by the Nilambur kōvilakam, fasts, faces the sanctum, raises his trunk in salute and collapses on Guruvāyūr Ekādaśī day

title: Guruvāyūr Satyāgraha (1931–32 CE) and temple entry (June 1947)
description: K. Kelappan leads the landmark temple-entry campaign with A. K. Gopalan and P. Krishna Pillai, and entry for all Hindus follows in June 1947

title: Haibatrāvbābā organizes the pālkhī system (late 18th–early 19th c.)
description: the Scindia courtier Haibatrāvbābā Ārphaḷkar reorganizes the Jñāneśvar pālkhī from Āḷandī with its diṇḍī register, horses and staged halts, creating the modern Wārī order

title: Hanumān darśana at Vārāṇasī and Citrakūṭ
description: a grateful preta points Tulsī to Hanumān disguised as a leper at his kathā; Hanumān then grants him the sight of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at Citrakūṭ's ghāṭ, sealed by the parrot-sung tilaka dohā

title: Harbhuji Sankhla blesses Rao Jodha
description: the warrior-turned-Nath-disciple of Bhundel, one of the five pirs, by tradition blesses Rao Jodha's recovery of Mandore (mid-15th c. synchronism) before Jodhpur's founding [folk] [disputed]

title: Harṣa's court-comedy sequels
description: the emperor-playwright Harṣa sets Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā in Udayana's Kauśāmbī, adding a new beloved with Vāsavadattā already installed as senior queen

title: Harṣola copper-plates name the Nāgaras (949 CE)
description: Rāṣṭrakūṭa grants record Nāgara Brāhmaṇas 'come from Ānandapura,' proving the community established centuries before the charter-myth's fullest form

title: Havelī sevā and the pan-North-Indian song
description: The Madhurāṣṭakam becomes a staple of Puṣṭimārga *aṣṭa-yāma sevā* and spreads across the Braj Kṛṣṇa-bhakti world as a beloved sung stotra

title: Head of the sāḍe-tīn circuit
description: Tuljapur is reckoned the first of the three-and-a-half Śakti Pīṭhas of Maharashtra with Kolhapur, Māhūr and Saptaśṛṅgī, a living regional pilgrimage circuit
actors: the pilgrims of the Marathi country
source: Wikipedia, Three and a half Shakti Peethas

title: Hindu Succession Act absorbs the schools
description: the Mitākṣarā–Dāyabhāga divide that governed pre-modern Hindu inheritance is largely superseded by statute, with the coparcenary opened to daughters only in 2005

title: Hita Harivaṃśa founds the Rādhā-vallabha Sampradāya
description: the 16th-c. saint (trad. 1502–1552), initiated by Rādhā in a dream, establishes the order worshipping Rādhā as supreme with Kṛṣṇa as her servant, singing the Hita-caurāsī

title: Hitopadeśa attested
description: Nārāyaṇa's four-book Bengal reworking of the Panchatantra (with Kāmandaki's Nītisāra), composed c. 800–1373 CE with its earliest manuscript dated 1373 CE [scholarly]

title: Imperial imprisonment and the monkey siege
description: summoned to Delhi and jailed for refusing to perform a miracle, Tulsī is freed when hordes of monkeys ransack the court; a popular telling has him compose the Hanumān Cālīsā's forty verses in forty days of this imprisonment

title: Independent recensions by Śivadāsa and Jambhaladatta
description: Two further Sanskrit versions (c. 11th–14th c. CE) recast the cycle, Śivadāsa naming the hero Vikramāditya and Jambhaladatta substituting tales of his own [scholarly]

title: Initiation by Narharidās at Sūkarakṣetra
description: the orphaned Rāmbolā is adopted and initiated by the Rāmānandī ascetic Narharidās, who recites the Rāma-story to him at Sūkarakheta (Soron) — the one episode Tulsī himself corroborates

title: Initiation by the sweeper-siddha
description: convinced at last, Gopīcandra renounces the throne and takes Nāth initiation from the low-caste Hāḍi-siddha, the king's pride broken to receive a scavenger as guru

title: Jābāla Upaniṣad codifies immediate renunciation
description: the earliest major Sannyāsa Upaniṣad (last centuries BCE–early CE [scholarly]) rules that one may go forth the very day detachment dawns, and scripts the praiṣa formula

title: Jagannātha Dāsa's Odia Bhāgabata and the bhāgabata-tuṅgī
description: the navākṣarī-metre Bhāgavata becomes Odisha's household scripture, read nightly in village reading-houses, 16th century CE [scholarly]

title: Jagannātha rejects the Abhinava-Gīta-Govinda (15th c.)
description: Gajapati Puruṣottama Deva's imitation poem is laid overnight before Jagannātha, who keeps Jayadeva's original and casts the king's aside [regional] [oral tradition]

title: Jagannātha rides to Kāñcī for Puruṣottama Deva
description: the Kāñcī-Kāverī legend: two divine horsemen precede the Gajapati's army, pay the milkmaid Māṇikā with a ring, and Padmāvatī weds the 'sweeper' king at Ratha Yātrā, attached to r. c. 1467–1497 [regional] [folk]
source: Mādaḷā Pāñji tradition; Odia kāvya retellings

title: Jahāṅgīr and the founding of the Nadia Rāj
description: delivered by Annadā's power at the imperial court, Bhavānanda receives honours and zamindari rights from Emperor Jahāṅgīr, the poem's charter-myth for Kṛṣṇacandra's dynasty

title: Jain Candraṇakhā variant composed
description: Vimalasūri's Paümacariya (c. 4th–5th c. CE [scholarly]) recasts her as Candraṇakhā, mother of Śambūka accidentally slain by Lakṣmaṇa, with no mutilation

title: Jain inversion of Sītā's birth composed
description: Guṇabhadra's Uttarapurāṇa (9th c. CE) and Saṅghadāsa's Vasudevahiṇḍī record the Sītā-as-Mandodarī's-daughter variant [scholarly]

title: Jayaratha writes the Tantrāloka-viveka
description: the indispensable commentary preserving the school's lost lineage history (c. 12th–13th c. CE [scholarly])

title: Jayatīrtha's conversion and sannyāsa
description: the cavalry noble Dhoṇḍo Pant, awakened at the Bhīmā river to his past birth as the bullock that carried Madhva's books, takes ordination from Akṣobhya Tīrtha, mid-14th c. CE [scholarly]
source: matha hagiography; Sharma, History of the Dvaita School

title: Jyeṣṭhā Aṣṭamī and the Pandit exodus
description: Kṣīr Bhavānī's Jyeṣṭhā Aṣṭamī mela at Tulmul becomes, after the 1990 Kashmiri Pandit exodus, the diaspora's chief pilgrimage-anchor and emblem of return

title: Kabīr's anti-pilgrimage critique (15th c. CE)
description: the Banaras weaver-sant mocks bathing-piety and reportedly dies at cursed Maghar to repudiate the Kāśī-death doctrine [oral tradition]

title: Kacchiappar composes the Kanda Purāṇam
description: Kacchiyappa Sivāchāriyar of Kāñcīpuram renders and expands the Skanda Purāṇa's Śaṅkara-saṃhitā into the six-kāṇḍam Tamil epic of the Sūrapadma war

title: Kadalī and the mendicant years
description: the former king wanders as a begging jogī and passes through the enchantress-realm of Kadalī that also ensnares Matsyendranāth, resisting by his guru's power

title: Kakshivat's danastuti to Svanaya Bhavya
description: the poet Kakshivat itemizes king Svanaya Bhavya's gift of cows, chariots and teams on the Sindhu, prime documentary evidence of the Vedic poet-patron economy [scholarly]

title: Kalhaṇa opens the Rājataraṅgiṇī with the Nīlamata
description: Writing in 1148–49 CE, Kalhaṇa names the Nīlamata among his sources and begins his chronicle inside its world — Satīsaras, Kaśyapa's desiccation, and the Gonanda kings

title: Kāḷi grieves her impaled son
description: the foster-mother Kāḷi rages and grieves and cannot save her boy from the stake, the mother-goddess forced to witness her son's execution

title: Kālidāsa flourishes under the Guptas
description: Kumārasambhava, Raghuvaṃśa, Abhijñānaśākuntala and Meghadūta composed c. 4th–5th c. CE [scholarly]; tradition instead seats him among Vikramāditya's navaratna (epoch 57 BCE) [late text]

title: Kalīla wa-Dimna rendered into Arabic
description: Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ translates the Pahlavi Panchatantra, c. 750 CE [scholarly], naming it for the jackals Karaṭaka and Damanaka and founding the western branch

title: Kaliṅga's maritime trading age remembered in the Tāpoi kathā [scholarly]
description: Coastal Odisha's early-historic-to-medieval sea trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, run by the sādhaba merchants and their boitas, survives as folk memory in the Tāpoi ballad and the festival cluster of Boita Bandāṇa and Bali Jātrā
source: histories of Kaliṅga maritime trade; Odia festival tradition

title: Kaliyan the chieftain turns robber to feed devotees
description: a Chōḷa warrior-chief of Ali Nāḍu, bound by Kumudavallī's vow to feed 1,008 Vaiṣṇavas daily, exhausts his treasury and takes to highway robbery to fund the sacred kitchen

title: Kālketu founds the city of Gujarāṭ
description: At Caṇḍī's command the hunter clears the forest, founds Gujarāṭ city with tax remissions for settlers, and institutes the goddess's worship

title: Kalkuḍa and Kallurṭi deified as a paired daiva
description: the wronged sculptor and his avenging sister die into godhood and are installed together, propitiated through the Tuḷu Bhūta-Kōla, with Kalkuḍa the tutelary daiva of the artisan castes

title: Kalkuḍa raises the Kārkaḷa Bāhubali
description: the master-sculptor Kalkuḍa carves and sets up the c. 42-ft monolith of Gommaṭeśvara (Bāhubali) at Kārkaḷa for king Vīra Pāṇḍya of the Sāntara dynasty

title: Kallurṭi burns the king's palace
description: hearing of her brother's maiming, the fierce sister Kallurṭi takes a terrible form and sets fire to the royal palace of Kārkaḷa, consuming the line that crippled Kalkuḍa

title: Kaḻuvēṟṟam — mounted on the impaling stake
description: the god is raised alive onto the pointed kaḻu and dies impaled, the prolonged agony that forms the ritual and narrative core of the whole katai

title: Kamban's sympathetic Tamil Śūrpaṇakhā
description: the Irāmāvatāram (12th c. CE [scholarly]) renders her wooing of Rāma in the beautiful Kāmavallī guise with courtly kāvya pathos and psychological interiority

title: Kāñcī conquered and Padmāvatī carried off
description: led by the two divine riders, the second campaign breaks the Kāñcī army from Kāñcī to the Kāverī, and the emperor brings Padmāvatī back to Purī as war-prize

title: Kāṇipākam as oath-court
description: the shrine becomes a regional truth-ordeal where disputants swear before Varasiddhi Vināyaka on pain of a perjurer being swiftly stricken, a quasi-judicial oath acknowledged even beyond the temple

title: Kaṇṇaki ascends as Pattini from the Chera hill
description: after fourteen days Kaṇṇaki rises bodily to heaven with Kōvalaṉ in a celestial chariot from Neṭuvēḷ Kuṉṟam, witnessed by the Kuṟavar hill-folk who resolve to worship her

title: Kaṇṇaki burns Madurai
description: the vindicated Kaṇṇaki tears off her left breast and hurls it over the city, commanding Agni to spare the good and consume the wicked; the goddess Maturāpati reveals the past-life karma behind the tragedy

title: Kaṇṇaki burns Madurai and ascends as Pattini
description: Kaṇṇaki proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent, curses Madurai to flames, and is deified as the chastity-goddess Pattini, later merged with Kodungallur and Attukal Bhagavati

title: Kāśī-khaṇḍa codifies the Divodāsa cycle
description: The Skanda Purāṇa's Kāśī-khaṇḍa, compiled c. 13th–14th century CE, fixes the Divodāsa–Śiva exile cycle in its received form [scholarly]

title: Kāttavarāyaṉ fostered by Kāḷi
description: a divine, cursed-born boy issuing from Śiva is given over to the black goddess Kāḷi, who rears him as her mischievous, low-born, trickster foster-son of the cremation-ground

title: Khadga Tikkana's charge and death
description: Nallasiddhi's Brahmin commander Khadga Tikkana attacks the Yadavas at Somasila, chases them to the Penna river, slays many heroes and falls in the field

title: Khullanā's persecution and chastity ordeal
description: The merchant's second wife, sent goat-herding in rags by co-wife Lahanā, wins Caṇḍī's protection and passes a public chastity ordeal by her grace

title: King Bhoja unearths Vikramāditya's lion-throne
description: the Paramāra king of Dhārā finds the buried siṃhāsana whose 32 curse-bound statuettes each tell a tale of Vikramāditya's magnanimity, barring Bhoja until the thirty-second tale releases them

title: King Sudarśana engages Viṣṇuśarman
description: despairing of his ignorant sons at Pāṭaliputra, King Sudarśana entrusts them to the brahmin Viṣṇuśarman, who teaches nīti through four books of fables

title: Kottarakkara Thampuran creates Rāmanāṭṭam
description: the danced Rāmāyaṇa cycle that grows into Kathakali, born (per legend) of the Zamorin's refusal to lend his Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam troupe (mid-17th c. CE) [oral tradition]

title: Kōvalaṉ executed over the anklet at Madurai
description: denounced by the thieving royal goldsmith, Kōvalaṉ is killed on the Pāṇḍya king Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ's untried order while selling Kaṇṇaki's jeweled anklet

title: Kōvalaṉ weds Kaṇṇaki at Pukār and falls to Mātavi
description: the merchant Kōvalaṉ marries Kaṇṇaki in the Chola port-capital, then squanders his fortune on the dancer Mātavi after her debut, leaving her carrying Maṇimēkalai

title: Kṛṣṇa completes the 'dehi pada-pallavam' verse
description: hagiography tells that Kṛṣṇa, in the bathing poet's form, wrote the half-verse asking Rādhā's foot upon his head and ate Padmāvatī's meal [oral tradition]

title: Kṛtyakalpataru compiled
description: Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra of Kanauj, writes the earliest great encyclopedic dharma-digest in 14 kāṇḍas, the template for all later nibandhas

title: Kṣemarāja writes the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam
description: 20 sūtras with auto-commentary distilling recognition philosophy for the untrained, opening "citiḥ svatantrā viśva-siddhi-hetuḥ" (c. 1000–1050 CE [scholarly])

title: Kṣemendra completes the Bṛhatkathāmañjarī (c. 1037 CE)
description: the Kashmiri polymath produces a terse verse abridgement of the Bṛhatkathā, roughly a third the bulk of Somadeva's later ocean

title: Kṣetrayya sings the Muvva Gopāla padams
description: The wandering 17th-century Telugu padam-poet of Movva composes slow erotic-devotional padams to Kṛṣṇa as Muvva Gopāla, the core abhinaya repertoire of the later Bharatanāṭyam tradition

title: KSTS printing and the Lakshman Joo revival
description: the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (1911 onward) prints the canon, and Swami Lakshman Joo (1907–1991) transmits it orally to modern lineages [scholarly]

title: Kulaśekhara Varman reforms Kūṭiyāṭṭam
description: the Cera king reshapes Kerala's Sanskrit temple-theatre of the Cākyārs (c. 10th–11th c. CE) [scholarly]

title: Kulaśekhara's snake-pot ordeal
description: to clear the Bhāgavatas of a jewel-theft framed by jealous ministers, the Cēra king-saint thrusts his bare hand into a pot holding a live cobra and withdraws it unbitten

title: Kumārī Ghar built and the Kumārī Jātrā instituted
description: the last Malla king of Kathmandu builds the Kumārī Bāhāl (1757 CE) and sets the living goddess's chariot procession within Indra Jātrā

title: Kumbakonam sung into the Tevāram
description: the Nāyaṉār saints glorify the town's Śiva shrines in the 6th–9th c. hymn-canon, making it a Paadal Petra temple-city of Chōḷa Nāḍu

title: Kurukṣetra-milana and the Ratha-yātrā
description: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas read the Purī chariot festival as this reunion re-enacted, the gopīs drawing Kṛṣṇa from Dvārakā back to Vṛndāvana, with Caitanya reliving Rādhā's ecstasy

title: Kusumā Mālin vindicates and frees Salhesh
description: The flower-woman Kusumā Mālin, who loves Salhesh, exposes the real thief through her wit and magic; Salhesh is freed and restored to honour and kingship, their cross-caste love left unconsummated in many tellings

title: Lakṣmīdhara compiles the Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa (c. 1110–1150 CE)
description: the first great dharmaśāstra digest of pilgrimage law, sifting māhātmya claims into rules of yātrā [scholarly]

title: Lalitāditya builds Mārtāṇḍa
description: the Kārkoṭa king Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa monumentalizes Kashmir's great Sūrya temple at Mattan, c. 725–756 CE

title: Living samadhi of Ramdev at Runicha (Ramdevra)
description: Ramdev takes jivit samadhi at Runicha, traditionally Bhadrapada shukla 11, V.S. 1442 (c. 1385 CE), aged thirty-three; the samadhi becomes the cult's center

title: Madhusūdana's bhakti reconciliation
description: the strict non-dualist Kṛṣṇa-devotee writes the Bhakti-rasāyana and the Gītā-commentary Gūḍhārtha-dīpikā, and (by legend) petitions Akbar's court to arm the Daśanāmī Nāgas

title: Māgha composes the Śiśupālavadha
description: 20-canto mahākāvya on Kṛṣṇa's beheading of Śiśupāla at the rājasūya, c. late 7th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Mahendravarman's cave-temples
description: the Pallava king Mahendravarman I cuts rock-temples with dedicatory inscriptions into the Tiruchirāppaḷḷi rock, the earliest hard evidence of worship on the hill

title: Mahiṣāsura-mardinī radio Chaṇḍī-pāṭh begins (early 1930s CE)
description: Bīrendra Kṛṣṇa Bhadra's dawn recitation of the Devī Māhātmya on All India Radio becomes the canonical acoustic opening of Mahālayā and Devī-pakṣa

title: Majapahit conquers Bali (1343 CE)
description: Gajah Mada subdues the island, grafting Javanese court religion, triwangsa caste usage and temple style onto the older Balinese base [scholarly]

title: Māmunigaḷ's year-long Īḍu kālakṣepam and the Śrīśailēśa taniyan
description: Raṅganātha appears as a boy and recites the invocatory verse honouring his teacher, c. 1430s [traditional]

title: Man-eating leopard of Rudraprayag killed (1926 CE)
description: Jim Corbett ends the leopard's eight-year predation on Kedarnath-road pilgrims [scholarly]
source: Corbett, The Man-Eating Leopard of Rudraprayag, 1948

title: Mānaveda composes the Kṛṣṇagīti
description: the Zamorin's eight-night Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam cycle instituted as votive offering at Guruvayur (1650s CE)

title: Mānaveda's peacock-feather vision and the Kṛṣṇagīti (c. 1652 CE)
description: granted a vision of the child Kṛṣṇa through Vilvamaṅgalam, prince Mānaveda is left holding a peacock feather and creates Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, the eight-night dance-drama offered at the temple

title: Māndappan driven from home
description: the wayward, quarrelsome Chekavar youth Māndappan is expelled by his father Kumarachan and leaves North Malabar for his uncle's house in Coorg (Kodagu)

title: Māṇikcandra taken by Yama
description: King Māṇikcandra of Rangpur dies at the hands of Yama's messengers despite his deathless yoginī-queen's power, setting the epic's premise that even a king cannot escape death without yoga

title: Manusmṛti enjoins the Brahma-muhūrta
description: the dharmaśāstra rule 'brāhme muhūrte budhyeta' fixes pre-dawn waking as a daily duty, c. 200 BCE–200 CE [scholarly]

title: Masilamani-Meyer documents the tale
description: Eveline Masilamani-Meyer's critical study, edition and translation, The Tale of Kāttavarāyaṉ (Harrassowitz, 2004), records the ballad and its impalement cult for scholarship

title: Mass Kanwar Yatra explosion (c. 1980s–2000s)
description: Ethnographers date the north-western yatra's growth from a small sadhu-and-elder practice into a many-million annual pilgrimage to the late 20th century [scholarly]
source: Vikash Singh, Uprising of the Fools, 2017

title: Maynāmatī's death-prophecy
description: the yoginī Maynāmatī, disciple of Gorakṣanāth, foresees that her son King Gopīcandra will die within days unless he abandons throne and wives to be initiated as a jogī

title: Medhātithi condemns widow-burning (c. 9th–10th c. CE)
description: The great commentator on Manu rules anvārohaṇa to be forbidden suicide, comparing it to the effective-but-adharmic Śyena sacrifice — the strongest internal śāstric rejection of satī [scholarly]

title: Medieval digests codify the tithi-vratas
description: Hemādri's Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi (13th c.) and the Nirṇayasindhu (17th c.) codify these observances, quoting a fluid "Bhaviṣyottara"; the kathās as recited are 19th–20th-c. printed pothīs [scholarly]

title: Mehaji Mangaliya falls in battle on Janmashtami
description: the Mangaliya Rajput hero of the panch-pir roster dies fighting on Krishna's birth-day, on which his fair at Bapini is held (trad. 14th c.) [folk]

title: Melpathur completes the Nārāyaṇīyam (27/28 Nov 1586 CE)
description: the paralysed Melpathur Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri sings one daśaka a day for 100 days before the deity, is cured at the closing vision, and dates the work by the kali-dina chronogram āyur-ārogya-saukhyam

title: Mhaskoba follows Kāmājī to Vīr
description: Kāḷ-Bhairava migrates from Sonāri in the Bhīmā valley to Vīr in the wake of his Dhangar devotee Kāmājī, where his blood-taking cult takes root
source: Mhaskoba of Vīr; Sontheimer, Between Ghost and God

title: Militarized akharas crystallize
description: the armed ascetic regiments of sannyāsins, including the nāgā orders, take their standardized form by the 18th century [scholarly], despite the traditional 8th-c. Śaṅkara attribution

title: Mitākṣarā written
description: Vijñāneśvara, at the Cālukya court of Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇī, composes the commentary on the Yājñavalkya-smṛti that founds the birthright (janma-svatva) school of Hindu inheritance law

title: Modern recovery of the Nīlamata
description: Bühler's 1877 manuscript report signals the text's importance, de Vreese's critical edition follows in 1936, and Ved Kumari Ghai publishes the standard study and translation in 1968–73 [scholarly]

title: Mokṣopāya composed in Kashmir (c. 950 CE)
description: An anonymous Kashmiri author composes the Mokṣopāya, the earliest recoverable recension of the Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha, later Vedānticized into the vulgate [scholarly]

title: Mpu Kuturan institutes the kahyangan tiga (c. 11th c.)
description: the Javanese sage organizes every Balinese village around three temples (Pura Puseh, Pura Desa, Pura Dalem), unifying the island's sects [traditional]

title: Mudiyettu inscribed by UNESCO (2010 CE)
description: The ritual dance-drama of the Dārika-vadham, performed by Marar and Kuruppu communities in central Kerala's Bhagavati kāvus, is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

title: Mukundarāma Kavikaṅkaṇa composes the canonical Caṇḍīmaṅgal
description: Fleeing revenue oppression at Dāmunyā, Mukundarāma is commissioned by the goddess in a dream and composes the masterwork under Bāṅkurā Rāy's patronage (c. 1590s) [scholarly]

title: Murugan catches the falling saint
description: before he strikes the ground Murugan arrests the fall, appears in grace, and cures his wasting disease

title: Muttuppaṭṭaṉ meets the Chakkiliyar sisters
description: a wandering brahmin in the Tirunelveli country is seized by love for the two daughters of a leather-worker, Bommakkā and Timmakkā, who mockingly refuse him

title: Muttuppaṭṭaṉ renounces brahminhood and works leather
description: the brahmin accepts every condition, takes up the polluting craft, tans hides and stitches sandals, living as a cobbler among cobblers

title: Nakhshabī casts the parrot into Persian
description: Ziyāʾ al-Dīn Nakhshabī reworks the cycle as the Ṭūṭī-nāma c. 1330–1335 CE, compressing the seventy tales into fifty-two nights on an earlier Persian Javāhir al-asmār (c. 1313–15)

title: Nakhshabī's Ṭūṭī-nāma
description: the Śukasaptati's seventy parrot-tales adapted into Persian, 1330 CE [scholarly]

title: Nambi Āṇṭār Nambi expands the saint-roster (c. 10th–11th c. CE)
description: the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvandāti, under Rājarāja I's canon-recovery, fixes the count toward the canonical 63 [scholarly]

title: Nandā becomes royal tutelary goddess of the hill kingdoms
description: the Katyūrī (c. 8th–12th c. CE) and then Chand and Garhwal Parmār dynasties adopt Nandā as kul-devī, installing her at Almora and Kot Bhrāmarī
source: Almora and Kot Bhrāmarī sthala traditions [regional] [scholarly]

title: Nandanar the Pulaiyar devotee
description: a bonded agricultural labourer of the Pulaiyar community at Ādhaṉūr, barred by caste from Śiva temples, serves the Lord from the threshold with leather, drum-skins and garlands
source: Periya Purāṇam, Tirunāḷaippōvār Nāyaṉār Purāṇam no. 18

title: Nārāyaṇ Mahārāj institutes the pādukā procession (late 17th c.)
description: Tukārām's youngest son begins carrying the sandals of Tukārām and Jñāneśvar in joint procession to Pandharpur, seeding the pālkhī tradition
source: Vārkarī tradition; Deleury, The Cult of Vithoba

title: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa writes the Tristhalīsetu (16th c. CE)
description: the 'Bridge to the Three Cities' (Kāśī, Prayāga, Gayā) caps the scholastic jurisprudence of tīrtha-yātrā, codifying muṇḍana, fasting and the on-foot rule [scholarly]

title: Nārāyaṇa composes the Hitopadeśa
description: the Bengal poet Nārāyaṇa, under his patron Dhavala-candra, reworks the Pañcatantra and Kāmandaki's Nītisāra into a four-book Sanskrit nīti-kathā

title: Narayana Guru consecrates the Aruvippuram Śiva
description: The Ezhava sage installs a Śiva-liṅga himself in 1888 — 'my Śiva, an Ezhava Śiva' — founding Kerala's anti-caste temple movement, later organized as the SNDP Yogam (1903) under the creed 'one caste, one religion, one God for man'
actors: Narayana Guru; Dr. Palpu; Kumaran Asan

title: Naunidhirāma's Sāroddhāra digest and its 1911 English translation
description: the later digest quoting a lost recension carries the tale as its ch. 7 and, via Wood & Subrahmanyam (1911), becomes the globally circulated form of the story [scholarly]

title: Nirartha founds Tanah Lot
description: the reformer-priest Dang Hyang Nirartha seeds Bali's chain of clifftop sea-temples to the sea-god Baruṇa, including the tidal-rock shrine of Tanah Lot

title: Nirṇayasindhu completed
description: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa of Banaras produces the standard authority on kāla-nirṇaya, fixing the correct calendrical time for every festival, fast and saṃskāra

title: Nishān padayātrā and sawāmaṇī
description: the living cults take shape: vow-keepers carry the triangular _nishān_ flag on foot to Sālāsar at the Chaitra and Āśvin Pūrṇimā fairs, and fulfilled petitioners at both shrines host _sawāmaṇī_ feasts in the auspicious savā (1¼) measure

title: Nityānanda narrates the legend at the shrine
description: travelling with the Bengali devotees toward Purī, Nityānanda Prabhu recounts the whole Sākṣi-Gopāla history at the temple, fixing it as a signature Gauḍīya tale later redacted by Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja c. 1600 CE

title: Oldest Svasthānī manuscript (1573 CE)
description: the earliest dated copy preserves a short Sanskrit core that expands over four centuries into the 31-chapter Nepali household recension

title: Olivelle's critical edition (2005)
description: Patrick Olivelle reconstructs an earlier text behind the medieval vulgate and dates the composition to the 2nd–3rd century CE as a single-redactor ring-structured work

title: Ōtēnan is felled by the gun
description: invincible with the sword, the young Tacōḷi hero is at last killed only by treachery with a matchlock firearm, the ballad's bitter comment that the gun ends the age of the blade

title: Pādukā-sahasram composed in one night
description: Deśika answers a poet's challenge with 1,008 verses on Raṅganātha's sandals, including picture-pattern verses [traditional]

title: Panchatantra core composed
description: Viṣṇuśarman's five nīti-fable books (frame: teaching King Amaraśakti's three dull sons in six months) take shape, c. 200 BCE–300 CE [scholarly]

title: Panchatantra embedded in the Kathāsaritsāgara
description: Somadeva of Kashmir retells the five tantras inside the Bṛhatkathā ocean-of-story, c. 1070 CE [scholarly]

title: Pāṇḍuraṅga-māhātmya recensions composed
description: the Sanskrit sthala-purāṇa of Pandharpur is transmitted in Skanda and Padma Purāṇa recensions as a medieval glorification of the living cult

title: Panjurli and Guliga reach a global audience
description: the film *Kantara* (2022) stages a climactic Guliga Bhūta-Kōla, carrying the Tuḷu daivas and their possession-ritual to worldwide attention

title: Paranjōti sacks Vātāpi
description: the Pallava general Paranjōti leads Narasiṃhavarman I's army to burn the Cāḷukya capital Vātāpi (Bādāmi), then renounces war to serve Śiva at Tirucceṅkāṭṭaṅkuḍi as Ciṟuttoṇṭar
source: Periya Purāṇam, Ciṟuttoṇṭa Purāṇam; [scholarly] c. 642 CE

title: Parāśara Bhaṭṭar heads Śrīraṅgam
description: Kūrattāḻvān's son succeeds Rāmānuja's line (c. 1122–1174 [traditional]) and converts the Advaitin Nañjīyar

title: Pārijātāpaharaṇamu and Bhāmākalāpam
description: the episode becomes a literary and dance classic in Nandi Timmana's Telugu prabandha at Kṛṣṇadevarāya's court and in Siddhendra Yogi's Kuchipudi Bhāmākalāpam

title: Periya Tirumoḻi begins with 'Vāḍiṉēṉ vāḍi'
description: the redeemed saint pours out six works of ~1,253 verses, the 1,084-verse Periya Tirumoḻi opening with the world-weary discovery of the Nārāyaṇa name

title: Periyāḻvār's Tiruppallāṇḍu on Garuḍa
description: after winning the Madurai para-tattva debate, Viṣṇucittar sees Viṣṇu appear Garuḍa-mounted and, fearing for God like a parent for a child, sings the benediction that opens the Prabandham

title: Persian Jūg Bāsisht translated for Prince Salīm (1597 CE)
description: Niẓām al-Dīn Pānīpatī renders the Laghu into Persian for the future Jahāngīr; Mīr Findiriskī and Dārā Shukoh's circle continue the Persian reception [scholarly]

title: Piḷḷai Lokācārya composes the eighteen rahasya-granthas
description: Śrīvacana Bhūṣaṇa, Mumukṣuppaḍi and Tattva-traya fix the doctrine of causeless grace, late 13th–early 14th c. [scholarly]

title: Po Nagar goddess sanctuary of Champa
description: the Cham enshrine Yang Pô Inâ Nagar at Nha Trang, identified in Sanskrit as Bhagavatī/Umā and depicted as Mahiṣāsura-mardinī

title: Poonthanam and the Jñānappāna (c. 1547–1640 CE)
description: grieving his infant son, Poonthanam takes the child Kṛṣṇa as his own and composes the Malayalam bhakti classic, the Lord declaring his bhakti dearer than Melpathur's vibhakti

title: Poṭṭan Theyyam of the meleri
description: the North-Malabar kāvu theyyam in which the possessed performer falls and rolls on a bed of live embers, embodying the casteless Śiva across caste lines

title: Prambanan raised to the Trimūrti
description: the Sañjaya-Mataram court builds Indonesia's largest Hindu temple, three shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu with their vāhanas and Rāmāyaṇa reliefs

title: Pratāparudra Deva inscription mandates the Gīta-Govinda at Purī (1499 CE)
description: a Jaya-Vijaya doorway inscription orders that only Jayadeva's songs be performed before Jagannātha, codifying the nightly aṣṭapadī sevā [scholarly]

title: Pratimā-lakṣaṇa — the iconography of the gods
description: Khaṇḍa III's image-making canon describes the multi-armed Viṣṇu, the four-faced Vaikuṇṭha, Sūrya, Śiva and the Goddess — a prime early source used to read Gupta and post-Gupta sculpture

title: Present Ramdevra temple built under Ganga Singh
description: the current temple over Ramdev's samadhi is completed in 1931 CE under Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner

title: Printed pothīs spread the pūjā across India (19th–20th c.)
description: mass-printed vernacular pothīs in Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati and Telugu make the Satyanārāyaṇa Pūjā the most widely performed household kathā of modern Hinduism

title: Prosperity and marriage in Coorg
description: the reformed Māndappan thrives as a merchant in Kodagu and weds his cross-cousin Chemmarathi

title: Pṛthvī Nārāyaṇ Śāh takes Kathmandu at Indra Jātrā and receives the Kumārī's tikā
description: the Gorkhā conqueror captures the city on the festival day of 1768 CE and takes the living goddess's blessing, transferring Taleju's royal mandate to the Śāh dynasty

title: Pūcalār Builds a Temple in His Mind
description: the penniless brāhmaṇa of Tiruniṉṟavūr, unable to afford stone, raises Śiva a complete temple entirely in his mind — foundation, walls, vimāna and liṅga imagined in Āgamic order

title: Pura Besakih, Bali's Mother Temple
description: a complex of ~23 temples on the volcano Gunung Agung, treated as the island's terrestrial Meru and chief of the Sad-Kahyangan sanctuaries

title: Pūrṇabhadra's Jain recension completed
description: the fullest surviving Panchatantra, 1199 CE [scholarly], today's de-facto vulgate and basis of most modern translations

title: Puruṣottama Deva's southern war
description: insulted as a 'sweeper' before Jagannātha's chariot and denied the Vidyānagara princess, the Gajapati king marches south, is aided by Jagannātha and Balabhadra as two warriors, and conquers the city
source: Caitanya-caritāmṛta, Madhya 5; Gajapati record, r. c. 1467–1497 CE

title: Rāghavendra enters the bṛndāvana alive (jīva-samādhi)
description: on a pre-announced day in 1671 CE [scholarly] the saint sits in meditation as the tomb-shrine is built over him, vowed to remain alive within it for 700 years [traditional]
source: Rāghavendra Vijaya tradition; Mantrālayam maṭha tradition

title: Rāghavendra Tīrtha's sannyāsa at Tanjore
description: the vīṇā-playing scholar Veṅkaṭanātha, chosen by Sudhīndra Tīrtha and commanded in a dream by the goddess of learning, is ordained in 1621 CE [scholarly]

title: Rāhu-kāla, Yamagaṇḍa, Gulika grid and Choghaḍiyā enter almanac practice
description: the eightfold weekday grid of inauspicious hours and the western-Indian choghaḍiyā system, unattested in classical siddhāntas, spread as late regional pañcāṅga practice [late text] [regional] [scholarly]

title: Rājā Salhesh enters Mithilā painting via the Dusādh godnā school (late 20th c.)
description: Dalit painters of the Madhubani region, most famously Chano Devi with Raudi Paswan, make the Salhesh cycle the central subject of their tattoo-derived godnā style, placing the Dusādh epic beside Rāma and Kṛṣṇa on paper
source: Mithilā-painting scholarship on the godnā school

title: Rājarāja I settles 400 dancing-women at Thanjavur
description: the Cōḻa emperor endows taḷicceri peṇḍugaḷ around the Bṛhadīśvara temple, the great epigraphic record of the devadāsī institution (c. 1004–1010 CE) [scholarly]

title: Ramalinga Vallalar founds the worship of the Grace-Light
description: The Tamil saint-poet of the Tiruvaruṭpā establishes the casteless Samarasa Suddha Sanmārga (1865), the Vadalur free feeding-house (1867) and the Satya Jñāna Sabhai (1872) where God is worshipped as Aruṭperuñjōti, a lit lamp behind veils, before vanishing at Mettukuppam in 1874

title: Ramana Maharshi renders the Dṛg-Dṛśya-Viveka into Tamil
description: the little seer-seen manual gains a wide modern readership through his Tamil prose translation, 20th c. CE

title: Ramaṇa Maharṣi revives the Tripurā Rahasya
description: praising the Jñāna-khaṇḍa as a supreme work on Self-inquiry, Ramaṇa Maharṣi has it translated into English at Sri Ramanasramam, carrying the once-obscure Śākta saṃhitā into the modern Advaita revival
source: Sri Ramanasramam; Talks with Sri Ramana Maharshi

title: Rāmānanda opens Rāma-bhakti at Vārāṇasī
description: c. 1400 CE Rāmānanda teaches Rāma-devotion across caste lines, seeding the Rāmānandī sampradāya, among the largest Vaiṣṇava monastic orders [scholarly]

title: Rāmānuja quotes the Keśidhvaja discourse
description: the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (c. 1017–1137 CE) cites Viṣṇu Purāṇa VI.5's definition of Bhagavat and VI.7's self-as-knowledge (jñāna-svarūpa) as proof-texts of Viśiṣṭādvaita

title: Rāmcaritmānas begun at Ayodhyā
description: Tulsīdās begins his Awadhi epic of Rāma on Rāma-navamī, V.S. 1631 (1574 CE), completing it in about two years and seven months across Ayodhyā, Kāśī and Citrakūṭ

title: Ratnāvalī's rebuke and Tulsī's renunciation
description: his wife Ratnāvalī shames the infatuated Tulsī ("had you such love for Rāma, you would have no fear of rebirth") and he renounces household life on the spot

title: Rebirth from the fire as Bhagavatī
description: by Śiva's grace the maiden rises out of the flames as a goddess and wanders the earth seeking a place to be received

title: Reborn as the spirit-children Nīli and Nīlaṉ
description: the murdered wife and her dead brother return as uncanny cattle-killing infants, abandoned tied to a karuvēl tree in the wilds of Pañcavaṉkāḍu

title: Rescue of Lachha Gujari's cattle
description: Teja pursues the raiders of Chang alone, recovers the herdswoman Lachha's whole herd, and is wounded over his entire body [folk]

title: Return after twelve years
description: his lifespan secured by yoga, Gopīcandra returns to Rangpur and to the enduring Aduna and Paduna, the prophecy vindicated as the king cheats death by having become a beggar

title: Roop Kanwar and the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act (1987)
description: The immolation of 18-year-old Roop Kanwar at Deorala and the mass glorification that followed prompt a law criminalizing both abetment and glorification of satī [scholarly]

title: Rukmini Devi founds Kalakshetra and renames sadir 'Bharatanāṭyam'
description: the revival re-frames the devadāsī art as a spiritualized concert form (1936 CE) [scholarly/disputed]

title: RV 10.85 codified as the vivaha liturgy
description: the Grihya-sutras fix Suryaa's wedding verses (the hand-clasp, the samrajni blessing) as the core of the Hindu marriage rite, mid-1st millennium BCE [scholarly]

title: Sābarṇa Roy Choudhury family pūjā begins (1610 CE)
description: the Barisha (Behala) household pūjā starts and runs continuously, commonly counted the oldest extant Durgā Pūjā of the Kolkata region

title: Sadānanda Yogīndra writes the Vedāntasāra
description: the standard compact prose introduction to Advaita (anubandha-catuṣṭaya, adhyāropa-apavāda, bhāga-tyāga reading of tat tvam asi), c. 15th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Sadāśiva Brahmendra, the silent avadhūta
description: the 18th-c. jīvanmukta of the Kāverī (samādhi at Nerur) writes the Ātma-vidyā-vilāsa and Yoga-sudhākara and composes the Sanskrit Carnatic kṛtis Manasa sañcara re and Pibare rāma-rasam

title: Sadukti-karṇāmṛta anthologizes Jayadeva (1205 CE)
description: Śrīdharadāsa's Sena-court anthology cites the poet, the earliest external anchor for his date and fame [scholarly]

title: Śākambharī of Sambhar
description: the Goddess becomes kuladevī of the Cāhamāna (Chauhan) dynasty, whose capital Śākambharī (Sambhar, Rajasthan) is named for her, ruling from there c. 6th–12th c. CE

title: Śākambharī Pūrṇimā cult
description: the living Śākambharī cult at Saharanpur, Sambhar and Badami (Banaśaṅkarī) observes the eight-day Śākambharī Navarātri and Pauṣa-full-moon Śākambharī Jayantī, offering vegetables to the food-giving Goddess

title: Sākṣī-Gopāla carried north
description: on the same southern campaign Puruṣottama Deva brings the Witness-Kṛṣṇa deity Sākṣī-Gopāla from the Vidyānagara country to Odisha, enshrined near Purī

title: Sālabega the yavana poet turns to Jagannātha
description: the Muslim subedār's son, healed of a mortal battle-wound after his Brāhmaṇ mother teaches him to call on Jagannātha, renounces arms to become Odisha's great bhajan-poet, barred from the temple yet singing 'Āhe Nīla Śaila'
source: Odia bhakta tradition; Sālabega's bhajans, 17th c.

title: Salhesh and Dinā-Bhadrī mobilised for Dalit assertion in Bihar (late 20th c.)
description: The hero-cults are consciously re-purposed as icons of Dusādh and Musahar identity politics — statues, memorial melās and printed hero-pamphlets — documented by Badri Narayan
source: Badri Narayan, Women Heroes and Dalit Assertion in North India, 2006

title: Salhesh deified as protector-god of the Dusādhs
description: The vindicated watchman-king is worshipped across Mithilā at gahwar shrines heaped with terracotta elephants, where possessed bhagat priest-mediums sing his gāthā and give healing and judgement

title: Salhesh falsely accused of the palace jewel theft
description: Rājā Salhesh of Mahisautha, serving as watchman of a royal fort, is framed for the theft of the royal jewels during his watch and imprisoned

title: Samadhi of Dali Bai
description: Dali Bai takes samadhi shortly before Ramdev; her tomb-shrine beside his at Ramdevra is by custom venerated first by pilgrims

title: Sambandar's Madurai contest (7th c. CE)
description: the child-saint cures the fevered Pāṇḍya and defeats the Jains in ordeals of fire and flood; the impalement of 8,000 Jains is doubted as history [disputed]

title: Sammakka's stand at Medaram and the vermilion casket
description: the Koya tiger-forest foundling-queen fights the Kakatiya tax-army at Sampenga Vagu, then vanishes into Chilakala Gutta leaving only a vermilion kumkuma casket and a promise to return every two years — origin of the biennial Medaram jatara, India's largest tribal religious gathering

title: Śāṇḍilya-vidyā taught in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad
description: the Vedic seer behind the sūtra-ascription teaches "sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma," c. 800–600 BCE [scholarly]

title: Śaṅkara at the Śāradā throne
description: Kashmir's Śāradā Pīṭha flourishes as a manuscript-university on the Kishangangā, its sarvajña-pīṭha ascended in tradition by Ādi Śaṅkara, c. 8th–12th c. CE

title: Śaṅkara composes the Upadeśa Sāhasrī
description: the one non-commentarial work of broadly accepted Śaṅkara authorship, a two-part (verse + prose) manual of direct Advaita instruction, c. 700–750 CE [scholarly]
source: Upadeśa Sāhasrī; Mayeda, A Thousand Teachings

title: Śaṅkara encounters the aged grammarian in Kāśī
description: Ādi Śaṅkara, walking Vārāṇasī with his disciples, comes upon an old Brahmin drilling Pāṇinian grammar (ḍukṛñ-karaṇe) as death nears
source: Bhaja Govindam / Mohamudgara frame-story; Śaṅkara-vijaya hagiographies

title: Śaṅkara encounters the old grammarian in Kāśī
description: Walking the lanes of Vārāṇasī with his disciples, Ādi Śaṅkara comes upon an aged Brahmin grammarian rote-drilling the Pāṇinian rule 'ḍukṛñ-karaṇe' as death nears him

title: Andal Discovered Beneath the Tulasi
description: The Alvar Periyalvar finds the infant girl Kodai (Andal) under a tulasi plant in the Srivilliputhur temple garden and raises her in Krishna-devotion, her earth-birth underwriting her Bhu-devi identity

title: Basava rejects the sacred thread
description: As a boy Basava rejects the Brahminical sacred thread (upanayana) in protest at birth-based hierarchy and leaves for Kudalasangama to study, taking Kudalasangamadeva as his form of Shiva

title: Bhagavata announcement of the Buddha-avatara
description: Vishnu foretold to descend as Buddha, son of Anjana, in Kikata (Magadha) at the start of Kali-yuga to delude the enemies of the faithful

title: Birth and identity of Bahiṇābāī
description: A Deśastha Brāhmaṇa woman, c. 1628–1700 CE, becomes a Vārkarī sant, distinct from the later 1880–1951 Khandeshi folk-poet of the same name
source: Wikipedia 'Bahina Bai'; Feldhaus, Bahina Bai: A Translation; Tharu & Lalita, Women Writing in India

title: Birth and life of Eknāth at Paithan
description: Eknāth, a Deśastha Brāhmaṇa householder-saint descended from Bhānudās, lives at Paithan on the Godāvarī as the pivotal mid-tradition Vārkarī figure (c. 1533–1599 CE)

title: Birth and marriage of Puṉitavati
description: Born Puṉitavati, devout daughter of merchant Taṉatattaṉ of Kāraikkāl, married to the merchant's son Paramatattaṉ

title: Birth and milk legend of Sambandar
description: Born at Sirkazhi to a Brahmin couple, the toddler Sambandar is fed divine milk by Pārvatī from a golden cup and sings his first hymn, earning his name

title: Birth and traditional dating of Sūrdās
description: Sūrdās, blind Braj-bhāṣā poet, born (trad. c. 1478 CE, near Delhi/Braj); scholarship favors an earlier, shorter 16th-c. floruit
source: Wikipedia Surdas; Britannica; Hawley; Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā

title: Birth as Nārāyaṇ at Jāmb
description: Born Nārāyaṇ Ṭhosar c. 1608 at Jāmb in Marathwada to a Deśastha Brahmin sun-worshipping family

title: Birth at Gangākheḍ and placement in Nāmdev's household
description: Janābāī is born to low-caste Vārkarī parents Dāmā and Karuṇḍ at Gangākheḍ on the Godāvarī and, after her mother's death, is placed as a maidservant (dāsī) in Nāmdev's Pandharpur household

title: Birth of Śaṅkaradeva
description: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva, founder of Ekaśaraṇa Dharma, is born into a Bhuyan Kāyastha family at Bordowā/Batadrava in Nagaon, Assam (traditionally 1449)

title: Birth of Bonbibi and Shah Jangali in Arabia
description: Bonbibi and her twin brother Shah Jangali are born to the fakir Ibrahim and his second wife Gulalbibi and abandoned in the forest, where Bonbibi is suckled by a deer

title: Birth of Nammalvar and the subduing of Shatha
description: Born Maran to a non-Brahmin Vellalar family, the infant Nammalvar subdues Shatha (the wind afflicting newborns), earning the title Shathakopa, and never cries, eats or speaks

title: Birth of Nāmdev into the śimpī community
description: Nāmdev is born (c. 1270) into the low-caste śimpī tailor/calico-printer community of Pandharpur, into a Viṭṭhal-devotee household

title: Birth of Ravidās at Seer Govardhanpur
description: Ravidās is born into a Camār (leather-worker / Dalit) family in a village on the edge of Vārāṇasī, c. 1450 CE (traditional)
source: Wikipedia Ravidas; Grokipedia Guru Ravidass Jayanti

title: Birth of the four prodigy siblings
description: Viṭṭhalapant and Rukmiṇībāī's four children — Nivṛttināth, Jñāneśvar, Sopāndev, Muktābāī — born c. 1273–1279 at Āpegāv/Āḷandī, all later venerated as saints

title: Birth to the courtesan Śyāmā of Mangalveḍhā
description: Kānhopātrā is born to Śyāmā, a wealthy courtesan of Mangalvedha, and raised in song and dance

title: Boy Śaṅkara on bhikṣā rounds
description: The young brahmacārin Śaṅkara goes house to house begging alms-food as a student-ascetic

title: Brāhmaṇa birth and child-marriage
description: Lallā is born to a Kashmiri Brāhmaṇa family near Srinagar and married young into a household at Pampore
actors: Lalleśvarī (Lallā); her natal Brāhmaṇa family; marital household at Pampore

title: Chandan Yatra (Chandana Yatra)
description: The 21-day sandal-paste boat festival opening the Puri Jagannath ritual year on Akshaya Tritiya: the representative deities Madanmohan (with Sri Devi and Bhu Devi) and the Pancha-Pandavas are rowed on decorated boats (chapas) on the Narendra tank and anointed with cooling sandal-paste against the summer heat; the same day chariot-building for the Rath Yatra begins

title: Childless couple's prayer for a child
description: The childless Brahmin illam-couple Ayyankara Vazhunnavar and Padikutty Amma perform austerities praying for a son
source: Parassinikkadavu Muthappan origin legend (theyyam oral tradition)

title: Chokhamela born a Mahar at Pandharpur
description: The first-tier Varkari poet-saint Chokhamela is born into the untouchable Mahar community at Pandharpur, a devotee of Vithoba
source: Wikipedia (Chokhamela); Varkari hagiography; Zelliot, From Untouchable to Dalit

title: Codification of the shared temple vocabulary (garbhagṛha, maṇḍapa, antarāla, vimāna)
description: The śilpa/vāstu corpus fixes the functional parts of the Hindu temple — womb-sanctum, pillared halls, vestibule, circumambulatory, plinth, crowning tower — as a single shared grammar laid on the vāstu-puruṣa-maṇḍala
actors: Śilpins/sthapatis; the architect-god Viśvakarmā (mythic source); Maya (asura-architect)
source: Mānasāra; Mayamata; Bṛhat Saṃhitā; Wikipedia (Hindu temple architecture, Garbhagriha, Mandapa)

title: Composition of the Hanuman Chalisa by Tulsidas
description: Goswami Tulsidas composes a forty-caupai Awadhi hymn to Hanuman as a vernacular devotional companion to his Ramcharitmanas

title: Composition of the Kakawin Ramayana
description: The oldest major Southeast Asian Rama text is composed in Central Java c. 856-930 CE, modeled on the Sanskrit Bhattikavya rather than Valmiki directly
actors: Anonymous Old Javanese poet (sometimes ascribed to Yogesvara)

title: Composition of the Nirvana Shatkam by Adi Shankara
description: Adi Shankara composes the six-verse Atma Shatkam distilling nirguna Brahman and neti-neti into the refrain Chidananda-rupah Shivo'ham
source: Nirvana Shatkam / Atma Shatkam (attr. Adi Shankara)

title: Composition of the Saundarya-lahari
description: The 100-verse Sri Vidya hymn to Tripurasundari is composed/transmitted in the mature medieval Shakta-Tantra stratum, traditionally ascribed to Adi Shankara
actors: Adi Shankara (traditional attribution); Sri Vidya tradition

title: Composition of the Venkatesha Suprabhatam
description: The Sri Vaishnava acharya Prativadi Bhayankaram Annan composes the four-part dawn-awakening sequence for Lord Venkateshvara of Tirumala
source: Venkatesha Suprabhatam (15th c.); Sri Vaishnava acharya tradition

title: Construction of Rājarājeśvaram (the Big Temple)
description: Rājarāja Chola I builds and consecrates the Thanjavur Big Temple c. 1010 CE, naming it after himself
actors: Rājarāja Chola I; the architect Kunjara Mallan Rāja Rāja Perunthachan

title: Cosmetic and decorative kalās catalogued in the Kāmasūtra
