description: Vātsyāyana lists body-adornment skills (Viśeṣaka-cchedya, Aṅga-rāga, Citra-yoga, Bhūṣaṇa-yojana) among the sixty-four arts, the classical anchor for ritual body-painting

title: Crystallization of the Nāth Sampradāya
description: The Śaiva Siddha-yogī order coalesces in the 12th–13th c. CE from earlier Pāśupata, Kāpālika, Kaula and Siddha cults, with Śiva (Ādinātha) as first guru

title: Ādi Śaṅkara installs Śāradā at Śṛṅgerī
description: On his digvijaya tour, Ādi Śaṅkara chooses Śṛṅgerī on the Tuṅgā river for the southern Śāradā Pīṭha and consecrates the goddess of learning as a sandalwood (candana) mūrti, founding the first of his four cardinal Veda-seats and making Śāradāmbā the presiding deity of the southern Śaṅkarācārya lineage

title: Dolā Yātrā / Dol Pūrṇimā
description: On Phālguna Pūrṇimā, Kṛṣṇa as Dolagovinda (with Rādhā/Lakṣmī) is rocked on a decorated swing-palanquin amid colored powder — the Vaiṣṇava counterpart to north-Indian Holi
source: Bhāgavata Kṛṣṇa-līlā substrate; Odisha Jagannāth ritual calendar; Wikipedia (Dol Purnima); Drik Panchang

title: Gorakhnāth's boon and Gugga's miraculous birth
description: The barren Chauhan queen Bāchhal pleases the Nāth siddha Gorakhnāth, who grants a guggal-fruit prasād by which she conceives the serpent-favored hero Gugga

title: Gorā Kumbhār's life and abhaṅgas at Ter
description: The potter-saint 'Gorobā Kākā' of Ter lives as a Viṭhobā-devotee in the founding Jñāneśvar–Nāmdev Vārkarī cohort, composing Marathi abhaṅgas drawn from the potter's craft
source: Wikipedia, Gora Kumbhar; Vārkarī abhaṅga tradition

title: Gugga deified as snakebite-protector god
description: Gugga (Gogājī / Jāharvīr Gogā), a Cauhāṇ-Rajput warrior-chieftain of the Hindi-Rajasthani belt (c. 11th-12th c. CE), is deified after death as the supreme snakebite-protector deity of the northwest, worshipped by Hindus as Gogājī and Muslims as Zāhir/Jāhar Pīr at the Gogāmeṛī shrine, celebrated at Gogā Navamī and sung in the Gugga-gāthā / Gugga kī ghoṛī cycle
actors: Zāhir Pīr); mother Bāchal; cousins Arjan-Surjan
source: Gugga-gāthā / Gugga kī ghoṛī (oral bardic cycle); Goga (deity) — Wikipedia

title: Indus Valley / Harappan Civilization
description: Mature urban Harappan civilization flourishes c. 2600-1900 BCE with planned cities, standardized weights, and an undeciphered script, with disputed claims linking it to Vedic culture

title: Jagannath Rath Yatra (charter procession)
description: Jagannath, Balabhadra, Subhadra and Sudarshana Chakra are pulled in three towering chariots from the Puri temple to the Gundicha Temple and back, the annual chariot festival of the Char Dham

title: Kabir found as an infant on Lahartara Lake
description: A Brahmana widow abandons the infant Kabir on Lahartara Lake in Varanasi, where the Muslim weaver couple Niru and Nima find and raise him, making him Hindu by blood and Muslim by upbringing

title: Karuppasāmi as Ayyaṉār's black gatekeeper
description: Karuppasāmi, the black guardian-god with aruvāḷ iconography, serves as chief lieutenant and threshold-gatekeeper of Ayyaṉār in the kāval cult
source: Ayyaṉār-Karuppu kāval cult tradition; Tamil kāval-deyvam tradition

title: Kulashekhara renounces his Chera throne for devotion
description: The Chera king-saint Kulasekhara Alvar abandons kingship and worldly desire for absorption in Vishnu, the royal-renunciation frame of the hymn
source: Mukunda-mala Stotra; Perumal Tirumozhi; Alvar hagiography

title: Lagadha's Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
description: Oldest extant Indian astronomical text, a ritual luni-solar calendar tracking Sun and Moon against the nakṣatras, with no zodiac
source: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; histories of Indian astronomy

title: Lakulīśa reforms the Pāśupata order
description: The Gujarat sage Lakulīśa (~2nd c. CE), regarded as an incarnation of Śiva, reforms the Pāśupata movement and authors the foundational Pāśupata-sūtra, renaming it Lākula-Pāśupata

title: Manasā born of Śiva (motherless from Pārvatī)
description: Śiva's seed/will quickens a lotus or clay snake-image in the netherworld, producing the serpent-goddess Manasā without Pārvatī

title: Mirabai's childhood vow to Krishna
description: As a child before an image of Krishna, Mira declares 'He is my husband,' making her later earthly marriage a formality over a prior spiritual vow to Giridhar

title: Mirkhshah's persecution of the Sindhi Hindus
description: The ruler Mirkhshah of Thatta threatens the Sindhi Hindus with forced conversion, granting forty days to decide

title: Māri as rain-and-death mother
description: Māriyammaṉ worshipped as the Tamil grāmadevatā who simultaneously sends and cures pox/epidemic and brings the monsoon rain

title: Naraharitīrtha pioneers Kannada devaranāma
description: Earliest recognized progenitor of Haridāsa song within Madhva's paramparā, reputed pioneer of Kannada devaranāma; fl. late 13th–early 14th c

title: Nathamuni Recovers the Naalayira Divya Prabandham
description: Nathamuni (c. 824-924 CE) recovers the lost 4,000 Alvar hymns by reciting Madhurakavi's verses until Nammalvar reveals the whole corpus, compiling and setting it to music as the Dravida Veda

title: Nimbarka traps the sun in a neem tree
description: To honor a sannyasi guest after sunset when ascetics may not eat, Nimbarka traps the setting sun (arka) in a neem (nimba) tree so its light lingers, earning his name

title: Pañca-loha & aṣṭadhātu codified as sacred image-alloys
description: The Śilpa-Śāstra tradition fixes the five/eight-metal alloys (copper-base with gold, silver, zinc, lead/iron) as canonical for dhātu-pratimā, keyed to deity

title: Pañch Kailāsh grouping of five Kailāsa peaks
description: Five Śaiva Kailāsa summits — Tibet's Mount Kailāsa plus four Indian Himalayan peaks — assembled into a single devotional pilgrimage pentad paralleling the Pañcha Kedār/Badrī fives
actors: Śaiva pilgrims; Śiva as mountain-abode deity
source: Wikipedia (Panch Kailash); regional yātrā tradition; Skanda Purāṇa & Śiva Purāṇa

title: Patañjali compiles the Yoga Sūtras
description: Patañjali composes/redacts the 196-sūtra foundational manual of classical Yoga (c. 2nd c. BCE - 5th c. CE), crystallising Sāṃkhya-with-Īśvara as the practical darśana of stilling the mind

title: Pālegāḍu terrorises Tirupati
description: A predatory local chieftain (Pālegāḍu) menaces Tirupati and its women, provoking Gangamma's resolve to destroy him

title: Puṇḍalīka tosses the brick
description: The devoted son Puṇḍalīka, absorbed in serving his aged parents, tosses a brick for the arriving Lord to stand and wait on, fixing Viṭṭhal's standing pose at Pandharpur
source: Pāṇḍuraṅga-māhātmya (Skanda Purāṇa / Padma Purāṇa); Vārkarī hagiography

title: Ramananda founds the Ramanandi Sampradaya
description: Ramananda pioneers the organization of north-Indian bhakti and founds the Ramanandi (Ramavat) ascetic order centred on Rama-Sita, accepting disciples regardless of caste, gender or creed and preaching in vernacular Hindi

title: Ram Mohan Roy founds the Brahmo Sabha
description: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founds the Brahmo Sabha at Calcutta on 20 August 1828, the rationalist monotheist precursor of the Brahmo Samaj and engine of the Bengal Renaissance

title: Rise of the aniconic Dharma Ṭhākur cult in the Rāṛh
description: The aniconic stone/tortoise god Dharma Ṭhākur emerges as a non-Brahmanical justice-and-fertility deity of lower-caste communities in western Bengal
source: Bengali folk and ritual tradition of the Rāṛh

title: Śaṅkaradeva creates the Sattriya complex
description: aṅkīyā nāṭ plays, bhāonā staging and monastery dance in the Assamese sattras (1449–1568 CE) [scholarly]

title: Sāraḷā Dāsa composes the first complete vernacular Mahābhārata
description: the 'Śūdra Muni' of Jhankada writes the 18-parva Odia epic under Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, c. 15th century CE [scholarly]

title: Sattriya recognized as the eighth classical dance
description: the Sangeet Natak Akademi completes the modern canon of eight forms (2000 CE) [scholarly]

title: Sax's Mountain Goddess published (1991) [scholarly]
description: William S. Sax's ethnography becomes the standard academic account of Nandā Devī, the dhiyāṇī theology and the Rāj Jāt

title: Sāyaṇa's Veda-bhāṣyas
description: Vidyāraṇya's brother Sāyaṇa produces the standard medieval commentaries on the Vedas, traditionally under Vidyāraṇya's patronage and direction

title: Self-immolation at Karivellūr
description: homeless, she stands on burning coals at the Karivellūr Śiva temple and has a passing Vaṇiya boy pour his temple oil onto the embers, dying in the blaze

title: She out-debates the pundits
description: the maiden defeats the Perinchellūr Mūtta Gurukkaḷ and his disciples in open Vedic disputation over successive days

title: Shobhabazar Rājbāṛi pūjā with Clive as guest (1757 CE)
description: after Plassey, Rājā Nabakṛṣṇa Deb mounts a spectacular palace pūjā attended by Robert Clive, template of the colonial-era zamindari-babu pūjās

title: Shravani Mela attested in colonial gazetteers (19th c.)
description: The Sultanganj–Deoghar water-carrying fair appears in 19th-century district gazetteers as an established annual mela, the oldest documented stratum of the practice [scholarly]

title: Siddhendra Yogī composes the Bhāmākalāpam
description: the founding dance-drama of Kuchipudi, bound to the brahmin boys of Kuchipudi village; Tana Shah's copper-plate grants them the village in 1678 CE [oral tradition/scholarly]

title: Sir William Jones translates Manu (1794)
description: under Warren Hastings the code becomes *Institutes of Hindu Law*, elevating Manu through Kullūka's vulgate into a pillar of colonial Anglo-Hindu personal law

title: Śītalā's cooling-the-heat theology
description: Śītalā both sends and cools smallpox, pox, measles and fevers, the eruptions read as her presence in the body and propitiated by cooling
source: North Indian folk tradition; vrata-kathā tradition

title: Śiva commands Nandi to shift at Tiruppuṅkūr
description: with the great stone bull blocking Nandanar's distant view of the liṅga, Śiva orders Nandi to move aside; the Tiruppuṅkūr Nandi stands off-axis to this day

title: Śiva crowns the boy Caṇḍeśa
description: Śiva and Umā manifest, restore the father's leg, adopt the child as their own, set Śiva's own head-garland on him, and name him Caṇḍeśa, chief of the gaṇas and eternal steward of Śiva's wealth

title: Śiva Orders Rājasiṃha to Postpone the Kāñci Consecration
description: in a dream Śiva tells the Pallava king Rājasiṃha (Narasiṃhavarman II) to delay dedicating his great stone temple, for the Lord must first attend Pūcalār's mind-temple consecration on the same day

title: Śiva Purāṇa's Nārada-moha frame compiled
description: the surviving Rudra-saṃhitā text containing the monkey-face story takes shape c. 10th–14th century CE [scholarly]

title: Śiva reveals himself and takes the household to Kailāsa
description: Śiva appears with Umā on Nandi, declares the test passed, and carries Ciṟuttoṇṭar, his wife, son, and servant to Śivaloka

title: Śiva takes service as the servant Ugnā
description: enchanted by Vidyāpati's nācārī songs, Mahādeva disguises himself as the destitute boy Ugnā and enters the poor poet's household as a servant, binding him to secrecy

title: Śiva's dream-command to the Tillai Dīkṣitars
description: arriving at Chidambaram and barred from the sanctum, Nandanar is admitted after Śiva appears in the dream of the Tillai Brahmin priesthood ordering them to kindle a sacred fire for his devotee

title: Śiva-Sūtras revealed on the Śaṅkarpāl rock
description: Śiva directs Vasugupta in a dream to a boulder on Mahādeva mountain that turns over to reveal 77 engraved aphorisms in three unmeṣas (c. 850–900 CE [scholarly])

title: Śivopādhyāya completes the Vijñāna Bhairava Vivṛti
description: the full standard gloss on the 112 dhāraṇās, proof of living Kashmiri exegesis into the 18th century [scholarly]

title: Slandered as unchaste and cast out
description: the pundits declare that only a non-virgin could know such bodily truth, break her betrothal, and expel her from house and caste

title: Slaying of the demon Bhairava
description: Ramdev destroys (or banishes) the rakshasa Bhairava who was devouring the people around Pokaran

title: Smṛticandrikā compiled
description: Devaṇṇa-bhaṭṭa produces the authoritative digest of the South, a chief source of the Dravida sub-school of Hindu law

title: Somadeva completes the Kathāsaritsāgara (c. 1070 CE)
description: the Kashmiri brahmin retells Guṇāḍhya's tale in 18 lambhakas and 124 taraṅgas for queen Sūryavatī, wife of King Ananta of Kashmir, to divert her mind amid court troubles

title: Somadeva composes the Kathāsaritsāgara
description: a Kashmiri Brahmin condenses Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī *Bṛhatkathā* into 18 lambhakas and 124 taraṅgas of Sanskrit verse, the anthology that fixes these stand-alone tales

title: Somadeva fixes the romance in the Ocean of Story
description: the Kashmiri poet Somadeva sets the Udayana–Vāsavadattā saga into Books II–III of the Kathāsaritsāgara (c. 1063–1081 CE), the surviving Sanskrit form of Guṇāḍhya's lost Bṛhatkathā

title: Somānanda founds Pratyabhijñā with the Śivadṛṣṭi
description: seven āhnikas arguing everything is Śiva, tracing his line to Tryambaka (c. 900–950 CE [scholarly])

title: Sontheimer maps the pastoral substrate
description: G.-D. Sontheimer's fieldwork among Dhangar singers (1960s–70s) yields Biroba, Mhaskoba und Khandoba (1976), arguing the Sanskritized Khaṇḍobā sits atop a living shepherd-god stratum

title: Spanda-Kārikās composed
description: the vibration doctrine unpacked in ~52 verses, attributed by rival commentators to Vasugupta or his disciple Kallaṭa (9th c. CE [scholarly] [disputed])

title: Śrī Śāradā Maṭha founded for women's sannyāsa
description: the Ramakrishna tradition establishes an independent women's monastic order conferring full sannyāsa at Kolkata in 1954

title: Śrīharṣa composes the Naiṣadhīyacarita
description: 22-canto Nala–Damayantī mahākāvya at the Gāhaḍavāla court of Kannauj, 12th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Stambheśvar Mahādev, the 'disappearing temple' of Kavi Kamboi
description: the modern coastal liṅga-shrine on the Gulf of Khambhāt is submerged by the sea at high tide and revealed at low tide, its darśana timed to the ocean rather than the bell

title: Subak water-temple landscape inscribed by UNESCO (2012)
description: Bali's irrigation-cooperative religion of Dewi Danu's water temples is listed as World Heritage as a manifestation of Tri Hita Karana [scholarly]

title: Subba Rao collects the longest Telugu ballad-cycle
description: T.V. Subba Rao's 1963–68 fieldwork and Sahitya Akademi edition recover some 20 of the reckoned 32 palm-leaf ballads, establishing Katamaraju as the longest Telugu oral epic beside Palnadu
source: Katamaraju Kathalu, ed. Subba Rao, A.P. Sahitya Akademi 1976–78

title: Sultanate sack of Śrīraṅgam; Lokācārya's last journey
description: Piḷḷai Lokācārya escorts the Namperumāḷ image south and dies at Jyotiṣkuḍi (1311 or 1323 raid [disputed])

title: Sundara digs the suraṅga to Vidyā
description: Sundara, Kālī-devotee prince of Kāñcī, courts the learned princess Vidyā of Burdwan through the flower-woman Hīrā and tunnels secretly into her palace-chamber to wed her by gāndharva rite

title: Sundarar and Cheramān Perumāḷ ascend to Kailāsa (hagiographic close, c. 8th c. CE)
description: Sundarar returns on a white elephant, the Chera king riding after him on a horse charged with the pañcākṣara

title: Sundarar and the padikāsu
description: the Nāyanār saint calls himself "servant of all born in Tiruvārūr" and receives Śiva's daily gold coin, marking the town as the heart of his Tēvāram corpus

title: Sundarar sings the Tiruttoṇṭattokai (c. 8th c. CE)
description: at Tiruvārūr Śiva's command and Viranmiṇḍar's rebuke draw out the 11-verse hymn naming the servants, seed-list of the 63

title: Sung in the Tēvāram
description: Tiru-jñāna-Sambandar and Appar glorify Sirappaḷḷi in the Tamil Śaiva hymns, marking Tiruchirāppaḷḷi one of the 275 Pāḍal Petṟa Sthalams

title: Sureśvara the Vārttikakāra
description: Śaṅkara's direct disciple (hagiographically the converted Maṇḍana Miśra) writes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya vārttikas and the Naiṣkarmya-siddhi, locating avidyā in Brahman and rejecting jñāna-karma-samuccaya

title: Svapneśvara composes the bhāṣya on Śāṇḍilya
description: the principal surviving commentary reads the sūtra through the Gītā, medieval date variously placed c. 13th–15th c. CE [scholarly] [disputed]

title: Swami Vivekananda meditates at Karnaprayag (1890s CE)
description: the wandering monk's recorded stay during his Garhwal travels [scholarly]

title: T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī publishes the Trivandrum plays
description: thirteen anonymous Kerala manuscript dramas identified as Bhāsa's lost works, 1912–15 CE [scholarly]

title: Tacōḷi Ōtēnan worships at Lōkanārkāvu
description: the Nāyar kaḷari-master of Tacōḷi Maṇikkōth, hero of the second cycle, propitiates his tutelary goddess Lōkanārkāvu Bhagavatī before his combats, his valour underwritten by the Devī

title: Takṣaśilā and Puṣkalāvatī as historical capitals of Gāndhāra
description: the eponymous epic cities correspond to Taxila (Bhir Mound/Sirkap) and Charsadda (Bala Hisar), joint capitals of the Gāndhāra mahājanapada named in Darius I's inscriptions c. 518 BCE

title: Taleju brought from Simraungadh to the Kathmandu Valley
description: with the fall of Simraungadh to the Tughlaq forces c. 1324–26 CE, the goddess travels north with Harisiṃhadeva's refugee dynasty and becomes the Malla kings' lineage goddess

title: Taleju temple of Kathmandu Durbar Square built
description: king Mahendra Malla raises the towering Taleju temple at Hanuman Dhoka, 1564 CE, opened to the public only at Mahānavamī of Dasain

title: Taleju's dice-game withdrawal and the Kumārī decree
description: offended by the king's desiring gaze (or the spying queen), the goddess ends her nightly dice sessions and decrees she will henceforth dwell only in a virgin Śākya girl — the charter of the living Kumārī (Malla-era legend, variously attached to Jaya Prakāśa Malla or Trailokya Malla)

title: Taṇḍiyaḍigaḷ deepens the Kamalālayam
description: the blind Nāyanār of Tiruvārūr enlarges the great temple tank against the mockery of Jains, one of the town's saints catalogued by Sēkkiḻār

title: Tantric flowering of the Vaṭuka cult
description: the developed boy-Bhairava worship — dhyāna, stotra, kavaca, and kṣetrapāla role — crystallizes in the Bhairava/Kaula/Śrī Vidyā stream across the medieval Tantric period

title: Tapas codified as a yogic niyama
description: Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras (c. 350–450 CE [scholarly]) list tapas among the niyamas and as the first limb of kriyā-yoga

title: Tāpoi born to the sādhaba house
description: A wealthy seafaring merchant of coastal Odisha, father of seven sons, gains a long-wished-for only daughter, Tāpoi, raised in luxury — even a golden moon commissioned as her toy

title: Tāpoi worships Maṅgaḷā with broken rice
description: Weeping over a lost goat, the persecuted girl offers the goddess Maṅgaḷā her only possession, a handful of khuda; the goddess restores the goat, takes her under protection, and promises the brothers' return

title: Teja Dashami and the Parbatsar cattle fair
description: Bhadrapada shukla dashami becomes Tejaji's festival, when tanti-vows are untied at his shrines and one of Rajasthan's largest cattle fairs gathers at Parbatsar [regional]

title: Tejaji's vow to the burning serpent
description: riding to Paner for his bride Pemal, Teja saves a naga from a fire and pledges to return and receive its bite once his errand is done [folk]

title: Temple entry opened to all castes (1947)
description: after the campaign associated with Sane Guruji, Pandharpur's Viṭṭhala temple admits 'untouchable' devotees, vindicating the ethic dramatized by Cokhāmeḷā's samādhi at the Mahādvāra

title: The 1772 Raṇchhoḍrāī temple
description: the Maratha noble Goplarāv Jagannāth Tāmbvekar builds the present temple on the Gomatī tank at Ḍākor

title: The 2004 Mahāmaham stampede
description: the modern twelve-year cycle (1992, 2004, 2016, next 2028) is marked by a fatal crush at the 24 Feb 2004 bathing that killed some fifty pilgrims

title: The 30-muhūrta day codified in the Brāhmaṇas
description: the ahorātra is fixed at 30 muhūrtas and the year at 10,800, with deity-named muhūrta rosters, c. 900–700 BCE [scholarly]
source: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa X.4.2; Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa III.10.1

title: The 32 statuettes halt Bhoja and free themselves
description: each apsara-statuette blocks Bhoja's ascent with a tale of Vikrama's magnanimity until, after the thirty-second, he concedes his unworthiness, and the nymphs' curse lifts and they return to heaven

title: The abduction of the Brahmin maiden
description: Kāttavarāyaṉ carries Āriyamālā off and takes her as his own, at once a love-match and the gravest defilement the caste order can name, provoking the Brahmins' outrage

title: The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa canonizes the robber-conversion legend
description: the family-refusal and marā-marā story enters Sanskrit literature c. 14th–15th c. CE, two millennia after the epic's core [scholarly]

title: The Advaitasiddhi
description: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī at Kāśī writes the point-by-point refutation of Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta, the high-water mark of the Advaita–Dvaita polemic

title: The Āḻvār hagiographies compiled
description: the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācāryas fix the saints' miracle-lives in Garuḍavāhana Paṇḍita's Sanskrit Divya Sūri Caritam (c. 12th c.) and Pinbaḻagiya Perumāḷ Jīyar's Tamil Guruparampara Prabhāvam 6000-paḍi (c. 13th–14th c.)

title: The Alvars Sing the 108 Divya Desams
description: The twelve Alvar poet-saints (c. 5th-9th c. CE) sing Vishnu shrines in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham, the act of mangalasasanam canonizing the 108 Divya Desams

title: The aṅkam of Ārōmal Cēkavar
description: hired to fight a chieftain's judicial duel on the aṅkattaṭṭu, the peerless Cēkava swordsman Ārōmal kills the veteran champion Aṟiṅṅōṭar but is treacherously stabbed at the moment of victory by his own cousin Cāntu

title: The anklet trial and the death of the Pāṇḍya king
description: Kaṇṇaki proves her anklet holds rubies against the queen's pearls; a ruby flies from the broken anklet, and Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ dies declaring himself the thief, his queen dying of grief

title: The annual Bhadwa mela at Ramdevra
description: lakhs of Hindu and Muslim pilgrims walk to Runicha for the fair running from Bhadrapada shukla 2 (Baba ri Bij) to the ekadashi samadhi day each monsoon

title: The armed Ālvār who sang the most divya deśams
description: the only Ālvār depicted with sword and consort, Tirumaṅgai dedicates decads to more of the 108 divya deśams than any other saint

title: The Ashtākṣara from the bridegroom's lips
description: the Lord whispers the eight-syllable Oṃ Namo Nārāyaṇāya into the robber's ear, initiating him and transforming Kaliyan into Tirumaṅgai Āḻvār

title: The bearded Bālājī ploughed up at Āsotā (1754 CE)
description: a Jāṭ cultivator's plough strikes a buried Hanumān image at Āsotā and his wife cleans it, revealing the unique daaḍhī-mūñch (bearded) icon of Sālāsar
actors: the Āsotā cultivator and his wife
source: Sālāsar Bālājī tradition, Śrāvaṇa V.S. 1811 / 1754 CE

title: The Bhairava's child-curry demand
description: Śiva arrives disguised as a fierce Bhairava/Kāpālika ascetic and demands to be fed a curry of a five-year-old only son, killed and cooked by the parents smiling and without grief

title: The Bhāmatī school named
description: the polymath Vācaspati Miśra (c. 9th–10th c. CE) writes the Bhāmatī on the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya, holding the jīva the locus of many avidyās and requiring prasaṃkhyāna-meditation alongside knowledge

title: The Bhavānī sword of Shivaji
description: Bhavānī gives (or is invoked over) Shivaji's celebrated blade, named for his kuladevī, charter of the Hindavī svarājya

title: The Bhavānī-sword legend of Shivaji (17th c. CE)
description: tradition holds the goddess appeared to Shivaji and gave him the Bhavānī talvār; historians treat the divine gift as legend, the kernel being a fine European blade named 'Bhavānī' for his kuladevī

title: The bhoṭo entrusted to Machhindranāth
description: the jewelled vest given by the nāga king to a Jyāpu farmer, stolen and disputed, is left in the god's keeping and displayed yearly at Bhoṭo Jātrā until a rightful owner proves his claim

title: The blind king variant
description: in one strand the Pārijāta errand is set to restore sight to a blinded king, an impossible task designed to make Aruṇagiri fail

title: The boita returns and Tāpoi is recognized
description: The seven brothers come home laden from the sea, find their sister a ragged goatherd at the landing-place, and hear from her everything the sisters-in-law have done

title: The brother slain a second time
description: woodcutters felling the acacia kill Nīlaṉ, leaving Nīli doubly bereaved and fixed wholly on vengeance as a shape-shifting yakṣi

title: The Buddha-birthday ordinance — an early Buddha-image rite in a Hindu text
description: The Nīlamata's festival catalog directs that the Buddha's image be bathed and śramaṇas honored on his birthday, the Buddha counted an avatāra of Viṣṇu — among the earliest brahmanical prescriptions of Buddha-worship [scholarly]
source: Nīlamata Purāṇa, festival ordinances, vv. c. 684 ff.

title: The buried guru Hāḍipā
description: the still-resisting king abuses his destined outcaste guru Hāḍipā, burying him in a dry well of filth, from which the siddha emerges unharmed by his yoga

title: The burning of six-sevenths of the Great Tale
description: spurned by King Sātavāhana, Guṇāḍhya reads the tale aloud and burns it leaf by leaf as the forest animals weep, destroying six of seven books before the king arrives to save the seventh, the Naravāhanadatta saga

title: The Caitra Pūrṇimā yātrā of Wadi Ratnagiri
description: the living cult of Jyotibā, with its pink gulāl, sāsan-kāṭhī processions and cry of "Cāṅg bhalā!", is documented medieval-to-modern regional practice on the Kolhapur hill

title: The calf-tribute repudiated
description: in the alternate cause, Katamaraju grazes Nellore's cornfields in breach of the pact, the queen destroys his herds unbeknown to the king, and he cancels the tribute as equal to his loss, triggering war

title: The Caṇḍikeśvara sub-shrine and the temple clap
description: every South-Indian Śiva temple sets an axe-bearing Caṇḍikeśvara shrine northeast of the sanctum, where devotees clap or snap fingers to show the steward they leave empty-handed

title: The Cāraṇ caravan attacked by Bāpiyā
description: A travelling Cāraṇ party including the woman Bahucharā is set upon by the marauder Bāpiyā, who threatens the women with abduction and dishonour

title: The Carnatic Trinity born at Tiruvārūr
description: Tyāgarāja (named for the deity), Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar, and Śyāma Śāstri are all born in the town, carrying its shrine into the Carnatic canon

title: The Champakulam idol and the boat race
description: the Krishna image is fetched by boat along the Pampa backwaters and halts at Champakulam, an arrival commemorated by Kerala's oldest snake-boat race, the Champakulam Moolam Vallamkali

title: The chariot halts for Sālabega
description: fearing he will miss the Ratha Yātrā, the ailing poet prays the Lord to wait, and Nandighoṣa stops dead on the Baḍa Daṇḍa, immovable by men or elephants, until Sālabega arrives for darśana

title: The Chola temple and the Āḻi Tēr
description: the standing Tyāgarāja temple is raised as a Chola foundation from the 9th c. (Rājendra I inscription, c. 1032), its ~300-tonne festival chariot the largest in Tamil Nadu

title: The Churning of the Sea of Milk carved at Angkor
description: the east gallery renders the Samudra Manthana ~50 m long: devas and asuras haul Vāsuki round Mount Mandara while Viṣṇu and his Kūrma avatāra bear the pivot

title: The Citrasūtra codifies Indian painting
description: Book III chs. 35–43, the earliest surviving Sanskrit treatise on painting, sets out the types of citra, iconometry, the rasas, the faults of a picture, and the preparation of pigments
source: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa III.35–43; Kramrisch, Part III

title: The cooking of Cīrāḷaṉ
description: the parents fetch their only son from school and, by the ascetic's terms, slay and cook him into a curry with unwavering serenity, then cook even the head at the guest's order

title: The couplet enters Vaiṣṇava liturgy
description: the "Vaiṣṇavas excepted" verse becomes a stock stotra citation across Śrī-Vaiṣṇava and Gauḍīya sampradāyas, paired with Ajāmila as proof the bhakta is beyond Yama
source: Viṣṇu Purāṇa III.7; later stotra tradition

title: The darbār of Bālājī, Pret-rāj and Bhairav
description: Mehandīpur's spirit-tribunal is constituted, with Bālājī as judge, Pret-rāj Sarkār (lord of ghosts) as sentencing magistrate, and Bhairav the Kotwāl as executing constable

title: The Deity carried to Odisha
description: Puruṣottama Deva brings the Sākṣi-Gopāla Deity from Vidyānagara to Kaṭaka (Cuttack), and by later temple tradition the image is moved to its present seat at Sākṣigopāl/Satyabāḍī near Purī

title: The disputed Viṭhobā substratum
description: Sontheimer reads even Viṭṭhal of Paṇḍharpūr as carrying a pastoral hero-stone origin beneath his Vaiṣṇava identity, an influential but contested claim

title: The double wedding among the leather-workers
description: having become a Chakkiliyar in work and life, Muttuppaṭṭaṉ marries both sisters by their community's own rites

title: The Dṛg-Dṛśya-Viveka emerges from the Śṛṅgerī circle
description: a 46-verse discrimination of seer from seen with māyā's āvaraṇa/vikṣepa powers, ascribed variously to Śaṅkara, Bhāratītīrtha, or Vidyāraṇya, c. 14th c. CE [disputed]

title: The Dutch raid on Guruvāyūr (1716 CE)
description: Dutch forces plunder and burn the temple, which is subsequently rebuilt

title: The dyūta-krīḍā carved in stone
description: the Umā-Maheśvara dice-play, Pārvatī turning away as she wins with Nandin looking on, is sculpted at Elephanta and Ellora from c. 8th c. CE

title: The Eran pillar, first satī inscription (510 CE)
description: The wife of the chieftain Goparāja, fallen in battle under Bhānugupta, follows him onto the pyre — the earliest dated epigraphic record of satī [scholarly]

title: The escaped elder and the seventy-two tally
description: in one telling sixty-nine burn and the fleeing elder is hunted down as the seventy-first, the phantom child making seventy-two dead

title: The false wife and phantom child at Palaiyanur
description: Nīli takes the exact guise of the merchant's wife and, weeping with a phantom infant, publicly claims him as her deserting husband before the village
source: Nīli Katai; source of the proverb 'Nīli's tears'

title: The father's kick and the axe
description: Yajñadatta (Echadattan), told his son is wasting the village milk, spies on him and kicks over the sand-liṅga; the rapt boy strikes at the offending leg with his staff, which turns to an axe and severs it

title: The fire-ordeal and merger with Naṭarāja
description: Nandanar enters the flames before the shrine and emerges a radiant sage with matted locks and sacred thread, walks into the Cit Sabhā, and merges into the jyoti of the dancing Śiva

title: The first campaign fails
description: insulted, Puruṣottama Deva marches on Kāñcī but is beaten back, and returns to Purī to reproach Jagannātha for abandoning his servant-king to defeat

title: The five pirs of Mecca and the flying bowls
description: five pirs test Ramdev, whose miracle brings their own bowls flying from Mecca; they bow and hail him Ramsa Pir, chartering his Muslim veneration

title: The flying cloth horse parcha
description: the child Ramdev mounts a tailor's toy horse of cloth and rags and flies into the sky, vindicating the accused tailor; the toy horse becomes his signature votive

title: The forced, flawed second Bāhubali
description: pressed to raise another colossus, the crippled Kalkuḍa cannot equal his first, and the second statue (the paddana's echo of the Vēṇūr Bāhubali) comes out smaller and flawed, sealing his ruin

title: The forgotten betel pouch
description: riding out against a Kodagu cattle-raid, Māndappan turns back home for his forgotten betel/pan pouch, the ill-omened return that hinges the tragedy

title: The forty-veli field ploughed overnight
description: set the impossible condition of tilling his master's vast field before leaving, Nandanar finds the forty-veli field ploughed by divine agency at dawn, and the astonished landlord releases him to make the pilgrimage

title: The Gaṅgā comes to the dying Vidyāpati
description: in the Maithili death-legend the aged poet halts short of the river and the Gaṅgā changes course to receive his last breath, the site remembered at Vidyapatinagar (Samastipur)
source: Maithili oral tradition; Vidyapatinagar local tradition

title: The Gaṅgā-water revelation
description: on a waterless road to Śivasiṃha's court the thirsty Vidyāpati tastes Gaṅgā-jala that Ugnā has secretly poured from his matted locks, and the servant is unmasked as Mahādeva

title: The garbo lamp-pot as cosmic womb
description: A perforated earthen pot holding a lit lamp (garbha + dipa) is danced around in concentric circles as the cosmic womb holding the Devi's indwelling shakti

title: The Garuda Purana's ratna-pariksha chapters are redacted
description: The gemology section retelling Bala's sacrifice is placed c. 800–1000 CE, with the Agni Purana's parallel gem chapter (246) in the same medieval horizon [scholarly]
source: Garuda Purana, Purva-khanda chs. ~68–70; Agni Purana 246

title: The Gautamī-māhātmya compiled into the Brahma Purāṇa
description: The ~105-chapter Godāvarī glorification, the Purāṇa's largest block, takes shape within the late compilation of the extant text (c. 10th–13th century CE and after) [scholarly]
source: Brahma Purāṇa, vulgate adh. 70–175; Hazra and later scholarship

title: The Gītā-Māhātmya composed as a Purāṇic appendix
description: the eighteen chapter-glorification tales are added to the Padma Purāṇa's Uttara-khaṇḍa as a late devotional phala-śruti, long after the Gītā itself

title: The god hidden in the Gomatī
description: pursued by the Dvārakā priests, Bodāṇā immerses the image in the Gomatī tank at Ḍākor on Kṛṣṇa's instruction

title: The Goddess Fed Second to Her Son
description: after Bāmākhepā eats Tārā's bhog and is beaten by the priests, the goddess appears in the patron-queen's dream refusing food until her hungry son is fed, so Bāmākhepā is henceforth fed before the Goddess

title: The gopuram leap
description: in self-disgust he flings himself from the north gopuram of the Aruṇācaleśvarar temple to end his life

title: The great temple fire (30 November 1970 CE)
description: fire destroys much of the complex while the sanctum and mūrti survive unharmed, and the temple is rebuilt under the Guruvayur Devaswom

title: The hunter-kathā fixed as the Śivarātri charter [scholarly]
description: the extant Śiva Purāṇa (c. 1000–1400 CE, Koṭirudra-saṁhitā), the medieval Kedāra-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, and the revised Garuḍa Purāṇa standardize the tale as the Mahā-Śivarātri vrata-māhātmya
source: Śiva P. Koṭirudra 38–40; Skanda P. Kedāra-khaṇḍa 33; Garuḍa P. Ācāra-khaṇḍa

title: The idol climbs the cart (1156 CE)
description: moved by Bodāṇā's frailty, Kṛṣṇa-Raṇchhoḍrāī mounts his bullock-cart and leaves Dvārakā for Ḍākor on the traditional date V.S. 1212

title: The idol-flights across the Zuari
description: as the Portuguese Old Conquests and the 1560 Goa Inquisition demolish the coastal shrines, mahājans secret the mūrtis of Mangeś (from Cortalim) and Śāntā-Durgā (from Quelossim) east into Ponda to rebuild worship

title: The Īḍu 36,000-paḍi is written down
description: Nampiḷḷai's Śrīraṅgam lectures on the Tiruvāymoḻi are recorded by Vaḍakku Tiruvīdhi Piḷḷai, 13th c. [scholarly]

title: The immolation of the seventy
description: true to their oath the seventy Veḷāḷa elders build a pyre and burn themselves, making 'the seventy of Palaiyanur' proverbial for a word kept unto death

title: The impossible tests are set
description: to prove his love the brahmin must cast off the sacred thread, eat beef, drink liquor, handle carcasses and tan hides — become a Chakkiliyar in full

title: The Jagdambā sword passes to Britain (1875–76 CE)
description: the Bhosale sword 'Jagdambā', popularly identified with Shivaji's Bhavānī sword, is presented to the Prince of Wales and remains in the British Royal Collection; the identification itself is contested

title: The Jagdambā sword to Britain (1875–76)
description: the Bhosale sword named Jagdambā, popularly identified with the Bhavānī sword, is presented to the Prince of Wales and enters the British Royal Collection

title: The kaḻu-tiruviḻā cult
description: worshippers of the northern Tamil low castes plant a stake, sing the katai and dance the god down into a possessed medium, the gibbet transfigured into the sacred post at his stake festival

title: The Kaumārikā-khaṇḍa composed
description: the Nandabhadra theodicy is set down as a sthala-māhātmya glorifying Mahīsāgara-Saṅgama near Cambay, a later medieval accretion to the composite Skanda Purāṇa

title: The Kaumārika-khaṇḍa retells the tale at Mahīsāgara-saṅgama
description: the Skanda Purāṇa localizes Indradyumna's redemption to the Kumārikā-kṣetra confluence, re-using the epic upākhyāna as tīrtha-māhātmya

title: The killer reborn as the guarded merchant
description: the murderer of the first birth returns as the trader Darśana Ceṭṭi (Āṉantaṉ of Kāverippūmpaṭṭiṉam), warded by a protective talisman against the pēy

title: The King Finds No Temple, Only the Saint
description: Rājasiṃha rides to Tiruniṉṟavūr to see the rival shrine and finds no building at all, only the poor brahmin, and bows on learning the temple was built within the heart

title: The Kommu bards and the Ganga Jatara
description: the cattle-war saga is sung across three months by Madiga Kommula-varu horn-bards and Golla minstrels to kommu, titti and talam at the Yadava goddess Ganga's village festivals, its fallen heroes worshipped as village deities

title: The Lalitopākhyāna and Sahasranāma reach written form
description: the Śākta appendix to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa carrying the thousand names is composed in the medieval Śrī-Vidyā efflorescence, commonly dated c. 13th–16th c. CE (some argue 9th–12th c.) [scholarly] [disputed]

title: The lament of Aduna-Paduna
description: Gopīcandra's two young queens break into the epic's most famous bilāp, mourning the living husband who abandons them for the jogī's road

title: The last darśana at Bhawanipur — origin of the Ugna Mahādev temple
description: Śiva consoles the grief-mad poet with a final appearance and remains present in the liṅga at Bhawanipur (Madhubani), the Ugnāsthān shrine thronged ever since at Śivarātri and Śrāvaṇa

title: The learned maiden of Perinchellūr
description: a prodigiously gifted Brahmin girl of the Maṇiyōṭṭu Mana near Taliparamba masters the Vedas and śāstra before her betrothal

title: The Liṅga Purāṇa redacts the Dadhīci legend under Śiva
description: the Śaiva Mahāpurāṇa (c. 5th–10th c. CE) reframes the pan-Hindu bone-giver's adamantine spine as a boon of Śiva and stages Viṣṇu's defeat, a sectarian charter for Sthāneśvara

title: The Liṅga Purāṇa's Śveta-upākhyāna composed
description: The Śveta chapter takes shape within the Pūrva-bhāga of the Liṅga Purāṇa, academically dated c. 5th–10th century CE with the doctrinal Pūrva-bhāga as the older stratum [scholarly]
source: Liṅga Purāṇa, Pūrva-bhāga ch. 30; academic dating [scholarly]

title: The love of Āriyamālā
description: Kāttavarāyaṉ sees the Brahmin virgin Āriyamālā and is seized by an impossible love, the untouchable-associated god of the burning-ground desiring the purest of the pure-born

title: The low-caste performer worshipped as god
description: once a year the Pulaya/Malayan performer, clad in areca-spathe and coconut fronds, is venerated by high-caste patrons as living Poṭṭan Daivam

title: The Madras Devadasis Act abolishes temple dedication
description: devadāsī dedication outlawed after the anti-nautch decades (1947 CE) [scholarly]
source: Madras Devadasis Prevention of Dedication Act, 1947

title: The maṅgal-kāvya literature of the goddess cluster
description: Manasāmaṅgal, Caṇḍīmaṅgal (Mukundarāma c. 1590s), Śītalāmaṅgal and the Ṣaṣṭhī bratakathās, composed 15th–18th c. CE by named poets [scholarly]

title: The mature muhūrta manuals composed
description: Muhūrta-Mārtaṇḍa (16th c.) and Rāma Daivajña's Muhūrta-Cintāmaṇi (1600 CE) codify marriage/saṃskāra election, gaṇḍānta and Bhadrā rules [scholarly]

title: The mendicant turns the sisters-in-law against Tāpoi
description: A wandering mendicant woman poisons the wives' minds; six strip Tāpoi to rags, feed her khuda (broken rice), and send her to herd goats, while the youngest sister-in-law alone stays kind

title: The Mental Kumbhābhiṣeka and Pūcalār's Ascent
description: Pūcalār performs the consecration of his mind-temple, Śiva attends true to His dream-word, and the saint at last reaches the feet of the Lord

title: The modern Nandā Devī Rāj Jāts (1905–2014)
description: the c. 280-km twelve-yearly royal pilgrimage from Nauti to Homkund, led by the four-horned ram, is held in 1905, 1925, 1951, 1968, 1987, 2000 and 2014 (postponed from 2013 after the Kedarnath floods)

title: The monolithic Hanumān of Suchindram
description: a ~18-foot Hanumān carved from a single granite block, once buried for protection and later re-consecrated, stands among India's tallest monolithic images of the god

title: The month-long Māgh recitation at Śālinadī
description: Nepali devotees, chiefly women, keep the Svasthānī vow through Māgh with dawn bathing at Sankhu and a chapter read each night for marital welfare

title: The Mughal illustrated parrot-books
description: Akbar's atelier illustrates the Ṭūṭī-nāma under Mīr Sayyid ʿAlī and ʿAbd al-Ṣamad after 1556, the manuscript now largely in the Cleveland Museum of Art, with a second copy c. 1580 at Dublin

title: The murder for gold (first birth)
description: a merchant who weds a woman for her jewels sends her brother off for water and kills her for the treasure, and the brother hangs himself in grief

title: The Nāgapaṭṭinam golden Buddha funds Srirangam's third wall
description: short of money for Raṅganātha's temple, Tirumaṅgai carries off a Buddhist vihāra's golden Buddha and melts its gold to build Srirangam's third enclosure-wall

title: The Nāgara-khaṇḍa compiled (13th–17th c. CE)
description: the ~279-chapter Hāṭakeśvara-kṣetra-māhātmya is composed in strata and grafted onto the Skanda Purāṇa as a quasi-caste-purāṇa for the Vaḍnagar Nāgaras

title: The Nārada Purāṇa's Uttarabhāga māhātmya stratum is compiled
description: The Gaṅgā-tīrtha and vrata tale-cycle takes shape in the late, stratified Nārada Purāṇa — Hazra's 9th-century core with pre-11th-century accretions, Wilson dating the extant text as late as the 16th–17th century [scholarly]
source: R. C. Hazra; H. H. Wilson

title: The navaratna is welded to the nine grahas
description: Medieval jyotisha systematizes Bala's nine relic-gems into the planetary amulet (ruby–Surya, pearl–Chandra, … cat's-eye–Ketu), a later layer than the origin myth itself [scholarly] [late text]

title: The Nawab's covered plate and the grant of Mantrālayam
description: the Nawab of Adoni's test-platter of meat turns to fruits and flowers, and the saint receives the village of Manchāle on the Tuṅgabhadrā, mid-17th c. CE [traditional] [folk]

title: The Nellore grazing pact
description: Katamaraju covenants with Nallasiddhi, Telugu-Choda king of Nellore, for pasture in the Nallamala forest, agreeing (one version) to render every male calf born as tribute

title: The night boundary-patrol of Ayyaṉār
description: Ayyaṉār rides out on horseback by night around the village limits to drive off demons, epidemic, drought and thieves
actors: Ayyaṉār (kāval deyvam); the village; pēy/picācu spirits

title: The once-a-year orchid garland of the Salhesh phulbārī
description: At the annual Salhesh melā of Mahisautha (Jur Sital, Maithili new year), a rare orchid in the mālin's flower-garden is said to bloom for a single day, read by devotees as Kusumā Mālin's garland still offered to Rājā Salhesh

title: The oxen halt and Sālāsar is founded
description: the image is carried from Āsotā by bullock-cart and the shrine is raised where the oxen stop, Mohandās installing and serving the god as founder-saint

title: The paddanas recorded and the Bhūta cult studied
description: Tuḷu daiva-paddanas are transcribed from the 19th–20th c. and systematically analysed in Peter J. Claus's fieldwork and *Oral Epics of India* (1989), framing bhūta-worship as a pre-Vedic Dravidian substratum

title: The Pañcasakhā circle flourishes at Purī
description: five Odia poet-friends develop jñāna-miśra bhakti and the Śūnya Puruṣa doctrine, overlapping Caitanya's Purī years 1510–1533 [regional] [scholarly]

title: The panch-pir couplet canonizes the five pirs
description: Rajasthani oral tradition fixes the roster Pabuji, Harbhuji, Ramdev, Mangaliya Meha and Gogaji as the pancho pir of Marwar [folk] [regional]

title: The parrot and the broken pact
description: Kundamadevi's tame parrot is shot in the grazing-forest, she sends hunters to slaughter the Yadava cattle, and Katamaraju kills the hunters, refuses the grazing-tax and fortifies at Yerragaddapadu

title: The parrot errand for the Pārijāta
description: set to fetch the celestial Pārijāta flower, Aruṇagiri projects his soul into a parrot's body to fly to Devaloka

title: The Pātāla-khaṇḍa's Puruṣottama māhātmya is composed
description: the Rāma-aśvamedha stratum of the Padma Purāṇa carrying the Ratnagrīva cycle takes shape as a late devotional layer, within the Purāṇa's c. 4th–15th c. CE compilation [scholarly]

title: The perpetual pal-payasam
description: the temple's milk-rice pudding is offered to the deity and ladled free to all pilgrims daily, the never-exhausted repayment of the chessboard debt

title: The peśī of the possessed
description: at Mehandīpur the possessing _pret_ speaking through a sufferer is compelled before the court to name itself, confess, and depart, the visible core of the exorcism cult

title: The petition-and-bell court at Chitai
description: the Golu temple near Almora institutionalizes divine justice: written petitions (traditionally on stamped judicial paper) are tied to the railings and granted prayers repaid with brass bells

title: The poet who took the deity's name
description: the Śaiva-Siddhānta poet-philosopher Tāyumāṉavar (c. 1705–1742 CE), a court official at Nāyaka-era Trichy, composes his Tamil verse and takes his name from the Rock Fort Lord (not to be confused with the god)

title: The Ponda temples rebuilt
description: the Śāntā-Durgā temple rises at Kavlem under Maratha patronage of Chhatrapati Śāhū (c. 1730s) and the Mangeśī complex at Priol through the 18th century, fixing the pantheon's living topography

title: The Pūrṇimā padayātrā
description: Ḍākor becomes a mass full-moon foot-pilgrimage centre, its Śarad and Phālgunī Pūrṇimā throngs re-enacting Bodāṇā's own journeys

title: The Puṣṭimārga aesthetic of *mādhurya*
description: The hymn enshrines Vallabha's choice of Kṛṣṇa's intimate sweetness over his majesty (*aiśvarya*), the devotional keynote of the Path of Grace

title: The question of pain and pleasure
description: trapped by the scholars, she answers that the greatest pain is childbirth and the greatest pleasure is the union of love — correctly, and fatally

title: The Ramnagar Rāmlīlā is instituted
description: the Maharajas of Banaras establish the 31-day town-wide Mānas enactment across the Gaṅgā from Varanasi (early 19th c. CE) [scholarly]

title: The replacement image at Dvārakā
description: Kṛṣṇa consoles the departing priests with a second idol found in the Gomatī creek at Dvārakā, fixing Ḍākor's claim to the original

title: The republic keeps the living goddess
description: after the abolition of the Nepali monarchy in 2008 CE, the President of Nepal attends Indra Jātrā and receives the Kumārī's tikā, the institution outliving the kingship it sanctified

title: The ring recognized
description: Māṇikā shows the ring to Puruṣottama Deva, who knows it for Jagannātha's own and understands the Lords have gone before him to fight his war

title: The Roopkund catastrophe (c. 9th century CE [scholarly])
description: legend holds King Jasdhaval of Kanauj and Queen Balampā perished with their party in Nandā's hailstorm for violating the pilgrimage's austerity; radiocarbon dating places many skeletons c. 850 CE, while 2019 aDNA found multiple groups including a c. 17th–19th-c. Mediterranean cohort [disputed]
source: Rāj Jāt legend [folk]; Harney et al. 2019 [scholarly]

title: The samādhi the Ratha still pauses at
description: Sālabega is buried on the Grand Road, and to this day the Jagannātha chariot halts each year at the Muslim-born devotee's tomb, the one such grave on the sacred processional route
source: Purī temple observance; Mādaḷā Pāñji lore

title: The sand-liṅga bathed in milk
description: the boy heaps a liṅga from river-sand and pours the cows' surplus milk over it in daily abhiṣeka, worshipping in total absorption

title: The Sanskrit kathā enters the Skanda Purāṇa's Revā-khaṇḍa
description: the five-chapter Satyanārāyaṇa Vrata Kathā, absent from older Skanda manuscripts, is interpolated under the Purāṇa's name in the early-modern period, with its precedence relative to Satya Pīr unresolved

title: The Satya Pīr pāñcālī corpus is composed (16th–18th c.)
description: over a hundred Hindu and Muslim poets, among them Phakir Rām, Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭācārya and Bhāratcandra Rāy, compose Bengali pāñcālīs of Satya Pīr carrying the woodcutter and merchant tale-blocks

title: The sculptor mutilated to prevent duplication
description: after the colossus is raised, Vīra Pāṇḍya has Kalkuḍa's right hand (and in fuller tellings a leg and an eye) severed so his hands can never make an equal Gommaṭa for any rival patron

title: The secret spoken — Ugnā vanishes
description: Vidyāpati's wife beats the servant in a household rage; unable to watch Śiva struck, the poet cries out that Ugnā is Mahādeva, and the god vanishes the instant the vow of secrecy breaks

title: The seven brothers sail on the boita
description: After the parents' deaths, Tāpoi's seven brothers depart on a long trading voyage across the sea, entrusting her to their seven wives

title: The seven-kanda Battle of Yerragaddapadu
description: Nallasiddhi invades with a huge army for a week-long war in which even the Yadava cows and oxen fight, led by the single-horned Vishnu-cow Bollavu
source: Katamaraju Kathalu, Battle of Yerragaddapadu, 7 kandas

title: The seventy Veḷāḷar stand surety
description: Palaiyanur's council of seventy Vellala elders, moved by her tears, disarm the merchant of his talisman and swear that all seventy will burn if harm befalls him

title: The short manuals Ātmabodha, Tattvabodha and Aparokṣānubhūti spread under Śaṅkara's name
description: a 68-verse primer, a prose catechism, and a 144-verse re-reading of yoga's fifteen limbs as Advaitic inquiry form the entry rungs of the Vedānta curriculum [late text] [disputed]

title: The Sinhala gammaḍuva ritual cycle for Pattini
description: Sinhala Buddhist villages honor Pattini, one of the guardian deities, in the post-harvest gammaḍuva, singing the pantis kōlmura and enacting the mango-birth and Palaṅga's resurrection

title: The sisters-in-law punished before the veiled 'goddess'
description: Tāpoi is seated veiled as Maṅgaḷā and each wife summoned to worship her; the six cruel sisters-in-law have their noses cut off while the kind youngest is spared and honored

title: The Skanda Purāṇa's Vaiśākha version is composed
description: the medieval Vaiśākhamāsa-māhātmya records the alternative conversion of the hunter by Śaṅkha and the rebirth as Vālmīki [scholarly] [late text]

title: The soul trapped in the parrot
description: Sambandāṇḍāṉ has the abandoned body cremated, so the returning saint remains in the parrot form — why his Tiruvaṇṇāmalai icon is a green parrot

title: The Suchindram Kaimukku ordeal
description: under Travancore rule the temple was the seat of a trial by ordeal in which the accused dipped a hand in boiling ghee to prove innocence, abolished in the modern reform era

title: The Suchindram Thanumalayan temple built
description: the standing Trimūrti temple near Kanyākumārī is founded c. 9th c. CE (Āy/Cēra era) and expanded under Vijayanagara-Nāyaka and Travancore patronage in the 16th–17th c.

title: The Śuka corpus takes textual shape
description: the Mokṣadharma Śuka-carita is fixed within the Mahābhārata (c. 200 BCE–300 CE), the Bhāgavata Purāṇa making Śuka its narrator is composed c. 8th–10th century CE, and the Devī Bhāgavata and Yoga Vāsiṣṭha retellings follow c. 9th–14th century CE [scholarly]
source: Mahābhārata XII; Bhāgavata Purāṇa; Devī Bhāgavata; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha

title: The Śukasaptati reaches its recensions
description: the Sanskrit parrot-cycle assumes its surviving shape by the 12th century CE in two parallel recensions, the plainer simplicior and the ornamented ornatior, descended from a lost common archetype

title: The svayambhu rock of Mehandīpur Bālājī
description: a self-manifest relief of child-form Hanumān emerges from the Arāvallī rock on the Dausa–Karauli border and becomes North India's foremost exorcism-court for the afflicted (_saṅkaṭ-wāle_)

title: The sweeper-king refused a bride
description: the Kāñcī king, seeing the Gajapati emperor Puruṣottama Deva sweep the chariots at the Chera Paṅharā, scorns him as a menial and breaks the betrothal of his daughter Padmāvatī

title: The Tanjore Quartet codifies the Bharatanāṭyam mārgam
description: Chinnayya, Ponnayya, Sivanandam and Vadivelu fix the concert format at Serfoji II's court (early 19th c. CE) [scholarly]

title: The temple tank dug overnight
description: by Śiva's grace Nandanar single-handedly excavates the Tiruppuṅkūr teppakkuḷam in one night so the god may have ablution water

title: The Teṅkalai–Vaḍakalai split hardens into rival kalais
description: doctrinal positions of the 14th c. crystallize into temple-controlling sects through the 15th–18th c., climaxing in colonial-era lawsuits [scholarly]
source: Appadurai, Worship and Conflict under Colonial Rule

title: The Thomas Munro apparition at Mantrālayam
description: legend holds the entombed saint emerged to converse (visibly to Munro alone) with the Collector of Bellary, who confirmed the maṭha's endowment in 1800 CE [folk] [disputed]

title: The Three Sangams convene at Madurai
description: By legend three successive literary academies meet at Madurai under Pāṇḍya patronage over ~9,990 years, the first two lost to floods (Kumari Kandam), only the third surviving

title: The Tiruppugazh composed
description: Aruṇagiri sings thousands of chandam-metered hymns to Murugan across his shrines, of which some 1,300+ survive of a claimed 16,000

title: The toe-ring that could not be lifted
description: Kaliyan strips the bridegroom's jewels but his hand freezes on the Lord's toe-ring (metti), which will not yield, revealing the groom as Viṣṇu himself

title: The tongue-bite and death of Tejaji at Sursura
description: finding no unwounded spot, the serpent bites Teja's offered tongue; he dies on Bhadrapada shukla dashami (trad. 1103 CE), Pemal becomes sati, and the naga's boon founds the tanti snakebite cult [folk] [disputed]

title: The twenty-day Brahmotsavam
description: Kāṇipākam observes one of the longest Gaṇeśa festivals, a roughly twenty/twenty-one-day Vināyaka Brahmotsavam from Gaṇeśa Caturthī with processional vāhanas and rathotsava

title: The twin dreams and Mohandās
description: the Āsotā Ṭhākur is commanded in a dream to send the image to Sālāsar while the saint Mohandās Mahārāj sees Hanumān the same night with the icon's exact marks, doubly sanctioning the transfer

title: The two-birds verse enters the Upanishads
description: RV 1.164.20 is taken over verbatim by the Mundaka (3.1.1-2, non-dual reading) and Shvetashvatara (4.6-7, theistic reading) Upanishads [scholarly]

title: The Upamanyu frame enters the written canon
description: The Anuśāsana Upamanyu–Sahasranāma block is a late Śaiva stratum of the epic (c. 200 BCE–300 CE), and the Śiva Purāṇa saṃhitās that enthrone him as frame-sage date c. 10th–14th c. CE [scholarly]

title: The Vajranābha romance enters the Harivaṃśa vulgate
description: the episode, absent from the BORI Critical Edition's constituted text (relegated to Appendix I), is judged a late accretion of roughly the mid-first millennium CE, yet preserves the earliest named play, cast-list and vidūṣaka in Sanskrit narrative [scholarly] [late text]

title: The varṇa-verse interpolation debate
description: Indologists from Colebrooke and Max Müller onward flag RV 10.90.12 (or the whole hymn) as late, while reformist and critical readers from Dayānanda to Ambedkar contest its meaning [scholarly] [disputed]

title: The Vel writes 'Muttai taru'
description: Murugan inscribes the seed of song on Aruṇagiri's tongue with the tip of his Vēl and gives the opening words 'Muttait taru', from which the first Tiruppugazh pours out

title: The Vetāla cycle fixed in Kashmiri Sanskrit
description: Kṣemendra's Bṛhatkathāmañjarī (c. 1037 CE) and Somadeva's Kathāsaritsāgara (c. 1070 CE) preserve the oldest surviving texts of the Vetāla-pañcaviṃśati, from Guṇāḍhya's lost Bṛhatkathā [scholarly]

title: The village as bounded sacred enclosure
description: Each village is conceived as a protected body with boundary/guardian gods at the edge and mother goddesses as its life, fertility and fever
actors: Boundary guardian gods; village mother goddesses
source: Henry Whitehead, The Village Gods of South India (1916); grāmadevatā studies

title: The Vīraṭṭāṉam shrines sung in the Tēvāram
description: the eight feat-temples enter the record as a set through the hymns of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, all counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams

title: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa reaches its received form, carrying the parable [scholarly]
description: Academic dating places the Viṣṇu Purāṇa's composition between c. 400 BCE and c. 450 CE, making the Ṛbhu–Nidāgha chapters a key pre-Śaṅkara witness to Purāṇic non-dual teaching

title: The Viṣṇudharmottara redacted
description: [scholarly] c. 400–600 CE the encyclopedic khila of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa takes shape, likely in Kashmir / the north-Indian northwest per Priyabala Shah, its arts book c. 5th–7th c. CE

title: The Viśvanātha temple vindication of the Mānas
description: Kāśī's paṇḍits, hostile to scripture in Awadhi, have the Mānas laid beneath the Sanskrit scriptures in the Viśvanātha sanctum overnight; it is found on top, endorsed "satyaṃ śivaṃ sundaram" by Śiva
source: Mūla Gosāīṃ Carita; Priyādās on Bhaktamāl [folk]

title: The Vivaraṇa school named
description: Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā, elaborated by Prakāśātman's Pañcapādikā-Vivaraṇa, founds the line holding Brahman itself the locus of one avidyā, the jīva a reflection, and mahāvākya-knowledge alone liberating

title: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi enters circulation under Śaṅkara's name
description: the ~580-verse guru–disciple 'Crest-Jewel of Discrimination' (brahma satyaṃ jagan mithyā) becomes the most famous Advaita manual; date and authorship post-Śaṅkara and unsettled [disputed] [scholarly]

title: The widows' lament and deaths
description: Bommakkā and Timmakkā find the body, sing the ballad's set-piece lament and follow their husband in death, joining him in the cult

title: The wives of Keteus contend to burn (316 BCE)
description: Greek historians record the two wives of the Indian general Keteus competing for the honor of the pyre, the younger prevailing — the earliest dated report of the practice [scholarly]

title: The Yādava-era temple
description: the standing shrine on the Yamunācalā, entered by descending flights to a sunken court, is assigned to the Yādava period (c. 12th–13th c. CE) with later Maratha rebuilding

title: Third jauhar of Chittor (1568 CE)
description: During Akbar's siege the women of Chittorgarh perform the last of the fort's three great jauhars before the men's final śāka ride and the fort's fall [scholarly]

title: Tipu Sultan's invasion and the idol's evacuation (1789–1792 CE)
description: during the Mysorean thrust into Malabar the utsava image is moved to Ambalappuzha and the main mūrti concealed, with worship restored after 1792

title: Tirtha Empul holy spring consecrated
description: the Warmadewa court founds Bali's great purification-spring temple, whose legend has Indra pierce the earth for amṛta against the tyrant Mayadanawa

title: Tīrtha-yātrā Parva stratum composed
description: the oldest systematic gazetteer of Hindu fords takes textual shape within the epic, c. 400 BCE–400 CE [scholarly]

title: Tirupati laḍḍu — prasāda as protected heritage
description: The Śrīvāri laḍḍu of Veṅkaṭeśvara, cooked in the Poṭu kitchen, receives a Geographical Indication tag in 2009, formalizing a mass annadāna economy

title: Tiruppāṇ carried on Lōka Sāraṅga's shoulders
description: struck by the priest's stone, the bard-saint is borne into the Śrīraṅgam sanctum on the archaka's shoulders, sings the Amalanādipirāṉ foot-to-face, and merges into Raṅganātha

title: Traditional immolation of Nārāyaṇī Devī, Rānī Satī (c. 1295 CE)
description: Rajasthani tradition dates the merchant's wife whose immolation founded the Rānī Satī Dādī-jī cult of Jhunjhunu, the largest living satī-mātā worship [folk] [regional]

title: Tribhuvaneśvara worshipped as Harihara
description: The Lingarāja swayambhū liṅga is worshipped simultaneously as Śiva and Viṣṇu (Harihara), receiving both bilva and tulasī

title: Trivikramasena outlasts the vetāla's riddles
description: carrying the corpse-spirit from the śiṃśapā tree twenty-four times, the king answers each riddle-tale, falls rightly silent at the last, and on the vetāla's warning beheads the treacherous mendicant Kṣāntiśīla

title: Tukārām born into Vārkarī devotion
description: Tukārām, a Śūdra grocer-cultivator of Dehu, is born to Bolhobā and Kanakāī into a Viṭṭhal-devotee family, inheriting Vārkarī devotion

title: Tulsīdās begins the Rāmcaritmānas
description: in 1574 CE at Ayodhyā, Tulsīdās starts the Avadhi retelling that anchors saguṇa Rāma-bhakti across North India [scholarly]

title: Tulsīdās frames the Rāmcaritmānas on Satī's doubt (1574 CE)
description: Composing the Mānas, Tulsīdās makes the Satī-test the motivating frame: Pārvatī, recalling her former birth's doubt, asks Śiva for the Rāma-story that becomes the poem [scholarly]

title: Tulsīdās retells the Nārada-moha in the Rāmcaritmānas
description: from 1574 CE the Bāl-Kāṇḍ recasts the tale (princess Viśvamohinī) as a cause of Rāma's descent, narrated by Śiva to Pārvatī

title: Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa Maṭha — the free meal and Kanakadāsa's window
description: Madhva's foundation institutionalizes perpetual caste-blind feeding; the kanakana-kiṇḍi window memorializes the low-caste saint for whom the image is said to have turned

title: UNESCO inscribes Durga Puja in Kolkata (2021 CE)
description: Durga Puja in Kolkata is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, cited for its fusion of religion, craft and public art

title: Uṇṇiyārcca routs the Nāṭāpuram rowdies
description: the warrior-sister of the Puttūram house, barred on the road to the Aḷḷimalarkāvu festival by a gang of Jōnaka toughs, cuts her own way through when her husband hesitates

title: Upaniṣadic and Purāṇic uptake of the Puruṣa theology
description: Śvetāśvatara quotes the "great Puruṣa beyond darkness" verse and the Bhāgavata elaborates the limb-cosmology into the virāṭ-puruṣa [scholarly]

title: Utpaladeva composes the Īśvara-pratyabhijñā-kārikā
description: ~190 verses in four books teaching liberation as recognition of oneself as Maheśvara, duelling Dharmakīrti's Buddhists (c. 925–975 CE [scholarly])

title: Vallabha composes the Madhurāṣṭakam
description: Vallabhācārya pours out the eight-verse 'Octet of Sweetness,' traditionally during his Braj *parikramā*, seeing all of Kṛṣṇa and his world as *madhura*

title: Varāhamihira systematizes electional astrology
description: the Bṛhat Saṃhitā's electional chapters anchor classical muhūrta-śāstra, c. 550 CE [scholarly]

title: Vasishtha's frog hymn composed
description: monsoon frogs croaking 'like brahmins around the Soma bowl' are praised as rain-bringers (or satirized priests), in the family-book stratum c. 1500–1200 BCE [scholarly]

title: Vengeance consummated
description: that night Nīli reveals her pēy form and kills the merchant, closing across two births the debt of the first-birth murder

title: Vicāra Śarman rescues the cows of Ceynalūr
description: a Vedic brāhmaṇa boy of Tiru-Ceynalūr on the Manni river, moved by pity for the village's abused cattle, takes over herding them himself

title: Videgha Māthava crosses the Sadānīrā — historical Videha emerges
description: The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's charter-legend of Videgha Māthava led east by Agni Vaiśvānara is read as memory of the eastward Vedic expansion that founded historical Videha (c. 8th–6th c. BCE) [scholarly]

title: Vidyāpati Ṭhākura of Bisfī, poet of the Oinwar court
description: the Maithili poet-saint (c. 1352–1448 CE [scholarly]) serves the Tirhut court of Kīrtisiṃha and Śivasiṃha and composes his trilingual corpus, including the Śaiva nācārī and maheśvānī songs

title: Vidyāraṇya at Śṛṅgeri
description: the 14th-c. Jagadguru, traditionally identified with the minister Mādhava who guided Harihara and Bukka in founding Vijayanagara (1336 CE), composes the Pañcadaśī and Jīvanmukti-viveka

title: Vidyāraṇya composes the Pañcadaśī at Śṛṅgerī
description: the 15-chapter medieval summa of Advaita in three pentads (viveka, dīpa, ānanda), with a co-authorship tradition naming his teacher Bhāratītīrtha, 14th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Vidyāraṇya formalizes vidvat- vs vividiṣā-sannyāsa
description: the 14th-c. Jīvanmuktiviveka systematizes renunciation-for-knowledge versus renunciation-of-the-knower and the jīvanmukta ideal

title: Vihari Lala Mitra's complete English translation (1891–1899 CE)
description: The four-volume Calcutta translation makes the full Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha available in English, still the only complete rendering [scholarly]

title: Vijayanagara enlargement
description: the Kāṇipākam complex is extended from the 14th century CE onward under Vijayanagara patronage, giving it much of its present scale

title: Vijayīndra Tīrtha's debates with Appayya Dīkṣita
description: the prolific Kumbakonam pontiff (c. 1514–1595 CE [scholarly]), credited with 104 works, contests the Śaiva-Advaita polymath in the Tanjore country
source: Sharma, History of the Dvaita School

title: Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra composed
description: Bhairavī questions Bhairava, who dismisses external forms and teaches the 112 dhāraṇās into undivided awareness (c. 7th–9th c. CE [scholarly])

title: Vikramāditya's Śaka victory and the Vikrama Saṃvat epoch (57 BCE)
description: tradition counts the era from the legendary Ujjain king's victory over the Śakas, though epigraphy shows the era first named Kṛta/Mālava and attached to Vikrama only from c. the 9th c. CE

title: Vīramitrodaya written
description: Mitra Miśra of Banaras compiles the multi-part digest named for his patron Bīr Singh Deo of Orchhā, a leading authority of the Banaras sub-school

title: Vīsaladeva grades the Nāgara sub-groups (13th c. CE)
description: a great sacrifice convened by the Vāghela king Vīsaladeva is credited with splitting the Nāgaras into their endogamous sub-divisions, dating the community's received shape

title: Vishnuprayag temple built (1889 CE)
description: the octagonal Vishnu temple over the confluence is credited to the Maharani of Indore [scholarly]

title: Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī waylaid as a wedding party
description: the Lord and his consort descend disguised as bridegroom and bride, leading a marriage procession through the robber's forest at Tirumaṇaṅkollai

title: Viśvanātha Cakravartī elaborates the prema ladder
description: the Madhurya-kadambinī walks the nine stages from śraddhā to prema and the Rāga-vartma-candrikā systematizes rāgānugā practice (c. 1700 CE [late text])

title: Viṭṭhala shrine inscriptionally attested (1189 CE)
description: the earliest secure epigraphic reference to the god's shrine at Pandharpur, followed by 13th-century Yādava-era temple expansion
source: epigraphic scholarship; Dhere, Rise of a Folk God

title: Viṭṭhalapant's renunciation and return to householder life
description: Jñāneśvar's Brāhmaṇa father takes sannyāsa, then on his guru's order returns to marriage with Rukmiṇībāī, a reversal orthodoxy held impossible

title: Vivekananda performs Kumārī Pūjā at Belur Maṭh (1901 CE)
description: at Belur Maṭh's first Durgā Pūjā, Swami Vivekananda worships young girls as the living Goddess, establishing the Ramakrishna Mission's famous Mahāṣṭamī kumārī-pūjā

title: Vivekananda preaches the Nārada sūtra's parā-bhakti (1890s)
description: the Bhakti-Yoga lectures carry the text into the modern revival, followed by Tyagisananda's standard edition [scholarly]

title: Vopadeva's Muktāphala maps bhakti onto the rasas
description: at the Devagiri court, Bhāgavata devotees are sorted under nava-rasa headings, a forerunner of bhakti-rasa theory (13th c. CE [scholarly])

title: Vulgate Harivaṃśa's Nikumbha–Ṣaṭpura cycle takes shape
description: [scholarly] the late Viṣṇu-Parva war cycles, judged appendix accretions by the BORI Critical Edition, reach vulgate form in the early-to-mid first millennium CE

title: Vyāsakāśī temple at Ramnagar
description: the c. 1750 CE shrine on Vārāṇasī's lone east-bank ghāṭ anchors the banishment legend, its sanctum holding three copper-cased liṅgas of Vyāsa, Śuka, and Viśvanātha

title: Vyāsatīrtha as Vijayanagara rāja-guru and the Nyāyāmṛta
description: the Dvaita dialectician (c. 1460–1539 CE [scholarly]) serves Kṛṣṇadevarāya's court, writes the Nyāyāmṛta that provokes Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi, and mentors the Haridāsas
source: Sharma, History of the Dvaita School

title: Wedded to the sweeping king
description: ordered to marry Padmāvatī to a sweeper in vengeance, the minister waits for the Ratha Yātrā and gives her to the emperor himself as he performs the Chera Paṅharā, honoring the order's letter while voiding its cruelty

title: Weighed against the nose-ring
description: the Gugli priests demand the idol's weight in gold; Gaṅgābāī's tiny gold nose-ring balances the black-stone god, and they must leave him at Ḍākor

title: Wilkins prints the first Sanskrit book in English
description: Charles Wilkins publishes his Hitopadeśa translation (1787), among the earliest renderings of any Sanskrit work into a European language

title: William Jones translates the Gīta-Govinda (1792 CE)
description: the first English rendering carries the poem to Europe among the earliest Sanskrit works known in the West [scholarly]

title: Wooing by disguise
description: using his shape-shifting trickster powers he approaches Āriyamālā in disguise and works charms to reach her across an impassable caste line

title: Xuanzang documents the Prayāga bathing assembly (644 CE)
description: the Chinese pilgrim records the great riverside gathering under king Harṣa, the earliest outside eyewitness of mass tīrtha-snāna [scholarly]

title: Xuanzang visits Ānandapura (640 CE)
description: the Chinese pilgrim describes Vaḍnagar as a walled, populous town, the earliest firm external date for the settlement the Nāgara-khaṇḍa mythologizes
source: Xuanzang, Records of the Western Regions

title: Yādava Prakāśa compiles the Yatidharmasamuccaya
description: the classic juridical digest of renouncer-law (rite, staff, begging, rains-retreat) is composed in the 11th–12th c. CE [scholarly]

title: Yādava-era Tuljapur temple built
description: the standing Tuljā Bhavānī temple fabric on the Bālā-ghāṭ is assigned to c. 12th–13th c. CE with Maratha-period and modern additions

title: Yājñavalkya's going-forth recorded in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka
description: the Upaniṣad (composed c. 8th–6th c. BCE [scholarly]) preserves the archetypal renunciation scene of Yājñavalkya leaving the household after teaching Maitreyī

title: Yajurveda redaction with the Uttaranārāyaṇa appendix
description: The hymn enters the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā as adhyāya 31 with six appended verses naming Hrī and Lakṣmī as the Puruṣa's consorts, c. 1200–800 BCE [scholarly] [late text]

title: Yamuna dies as Ramanuja arrives at Srirangam
description: Ramanuja is designated successor of Yamunacharya, the theological forerunner of Srivaishnavism, but the two never meet — Yamuna dies just as Ramanuja arrives at Srirangam

title: Abolition of sati (1829)
description: Ram Mohan Roy's campaign secures the 1829 abolition of sati, a landmark of rational reform under colonial modernity

title: Adi Shankara Founds the Four Amnaya Mathas
description: Adi Shankara founds four cardinal monasteries (Jyotirmath, Sringeri, Govardhana at Puri, Dwarka Sharada Pitha), each guarding one Veda and one quarter of India

title: Śaṅkara composes the refrain and rebuke
description: Moved to pity, Śaṅkara breaks into spontaneous song — 'bhaja govindaṃ … grammar will not save you at the hour of death' — coining the hymn's refrain and its message that only devotion rescues the soul

title: Śaṅkaradeva's pan-Indian pilgrimage
description: Orphaned and schooled under Mahendra Kandalī, Śaṅkaradeva undertakes a ~12-year pilgrimage to the tīrthas, then returns to propagate single-refuge Bhāgavata devotion

title: Akbar-imprisonment frame-legend
description: A folk hagiography holds Tulsidas composed the Chalisa while imprisoned by a Mughal emperor and was freed when monkeys besieged the court

title: Aniconic open-air shrine and non-Brahmin priesthood
description: Grāmadevatās are worshipped at open-air stones, termite-mounds, tridents and neem trees by non-Brahmin pūjārīs, not in Agamic temples by Vedic priests
source: Whitehead, Village Gods of South India; village-shrine ethnography

title: Bahucharā's tragu (self-mutilation)
description: Rather than submit, Bahucharā invokes the Cāraṇ right of tragu and cuts off her own breast, turning her shed blood into a sacred death-curse

title: Barred from entering the Vithoba temple
description: As a Mahar, Chokhamela is forbidden entry to the Vithoba temple and conducts his devotion from outside the threshold

title: Basava becomes chief minister to Bijjala II
description: Basava rises to treasurer and then chief minister of the Kalachuri king Bijjala II at Kalyana, using his state office to institutionalize the Sharana gatherings and fund the dasoha kitchens

title: Bengal Dol Pūrṇimā / Gaura-Pūrṇimā
description: In Bengal the swing of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa coincides with and doubles as the appearance day (1486 CE) of Caitanya Mahāprabhu, kept by Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas as Gaura-pūrṇimā

title: Bharata codifies svara, śruti, grāma, mūrcchanā and jāti
description: The Nāṭya Śāstra (chs. 28–33) fixes the seven svaras with animal-cry associations, the 22 śrutis (proven by the two experimental vīṇās), the grāmas, the 14 mūrcchanās and the 18 jātis

title: Bhāskararāya systematizes Śrīvidyā
description: Bhāskararāya Makhin (1690–1785) reconciles the diverse vidyās into one coherent Śrīvidyā philosophy, authoring 40+ works and founding a living lineage

title: Caṇḍī blinds Manasā in one eye
description: Pārvatī (Caṇḍī), hating the rival daughter, strikes and destroys one of Manasā's eyes, leaving her one-eyed (Kāṇī)

title: Childhood Viṭṭhal-bhakti and the milk miracle
description: As a child Nāmdev is said to have made the Viṭhobā image physically accept his milk/food offering, taking childlike love as true darśana

title: Child marriage to Gaṅgādhar Paṭhak
description: Married very young to a much older, orthodox, irascible Brahmin widower who bitterly opposes her devotion

title: Composition of the Dharma-maṅgal kāvya
description: Named Bengali poets compose the Dharma-maṅgal maṅgal-kāvya cycle (c. 14th–18th c.) to propagate Dharma-pūjā

title: Composition of the Mukunda-mala garland
description: Kulasekhara composes the Sanskrit Mukunda-mala, a garland of surrender-prayers to Mukunda (Vishnu/Krishna)

title: Ādi Kailāsh / Om Parvat darśana, Kumaon
description: The Chhota Kailāsh peak with its Pārvatī Sarovar/Gaurī Kuṇḍ lake and the neighbouring Om Parvat whose snow forms the syllable ॐ, pilgrimaged as a substitute Mount Kailāsa
source: Wikipedia (Adi Kailash, Om Parvat); Uttarakhand sthala tradition

title: Discipleship under Janārdana-svāmī
description: Eknāth studies under the Datta-devotee and fort administrator Janārdana-svāmī at Devagiri/Daulatābād and adopts the signature 'Eka-Janārdana'; tradition adds a vision of Dattātreya

title: Divine commission and arrival in the Sundarbans
description: The twins are blessed at Medina and commissioned by Allah to make the land of eighteen tides habitable; they arrive and claim the delta with the azan

title: Emergence of the Nāgara order and its sub-styles (Latina, Śekharī, Bhūmija, Kaliṅga)
description: The North Indian curvilinear-śikhara temple with āmalaka-and-kalaśa finials develops Gupta-onward, branching into single- and multi-spired forms and the regional Bhūmija and Kaliṅga (Odisha) sub-orders
actors: North Indian dynasties; Odia śilpins; exemplars at Khajurāho
source: Aparājitapṛcchā; Śilpa-prakāśa; Bhuvana-pradīpa; Wikipedia (Nagara architecture, Bhumija, Kalinga architecture, Shikhara)

title: Founding of the Kānphaṭa split-ear order
description: Gorakṣanāth organizes the Kānphaṭa ('split-ear') yogīs around the Gorakhpur maṭha, with the twelve panths and the Aughaṛ/Darśanī grades

title: Gangamma hunts the Pālegāḍu through successive disguises
description: Unable to confront him openly, Gangamma assumes a succession of veṣams (guises) to lure and corner the chieftain
source: Tirupati oral tradition; Handelman/Krishnamurthy/Dawson and Flueckiger ethnography [folk/scholarly]

title: Gathering of the sants at Goroba's workshop
description: A company of Vārkarī sants assembles at Gorā Kumbhār's potter's yard at Ter, where as the eldest he is asked to judge their spiritual ripeness

title: Gauḍapāda composes the Māṇḍūkya-Kārikā
description: Gauḍapāda, the parama-guru of Śaṅkara, composes the 215-verse Māṇḍūkya-Kārikā, the earliest systematic treatise of Advaita Vedānta with its ajāta-vāda doctrine

title: Indo-Aryan Migrations
description: Indo-Aryan speakers migrate into the subcontinent c. 1900-1500 BCE bringing the Indo-European language that becomes Vedic Sanskrit (disputed against an Out-of-India model)
source: History of India (Wikipedia); genetic studies (Reich et al.)

title: Kaṇṇaki burns Madurai (Cilappatikāram)
description: After her husband Kōvalaṉ is wrongly executed for theft, Kaṇṇaki proves his innocence and curses the city of Madurai, which burns down

title: Kabir descends from Satlok as a body of light
description: In the Kabir Panth's own account, Kabir descends from Satlok as a body of light and incarnates on a lotus in Lahartara Lake, witnessed by the rishi Ashtanand, marking him a divine avatara rather than a born human

title: Kaundinya's Pañcārtha-bhāṣya
